Line 4: 'aetates temporalium naturam' read as 'naturarum' (ages of temporal natures). 'Spiritus sanctus igniret' ('kindle'): some witnesses of Leo read 'ignosceret' or similar; rendered as printed. Scanning errors silently corrected throughout (e.g. 'S.pmtificis', 'hajusmodi', 'Reginæ Suecix').

Ch. VI: 'sine corde peccati' (printed text) is rendered as 'without the stain of sin', reading 'sorde peccati' (the usual Leonine phrase); taken as a scanning error. Ch. VII: the subject of 'est dissimilis' is unexpressed in the Latin; '[his nature]' supplied.

Ch. IX: the text appears defective after 'Negatur enim' (something like 'natura ... quae si' seems lost before 'necesse est'); translated with a bracketed supplement. Read 'dives' for 'divos', 'homo' for 'lio uo', 'assumpti, non assumentis' for 'ussumpti non, assumentis', 'illum exaltavit' for 'dium exsaUavit', 'exaltationem' for 'exultationem', 'actiones' for 'artiones'. Ch. X: 'tres varias protulerunt partes' is obscure; rendered 'produced three different factions'. The second scripture reference in Ch. X ('Joan. xix') should be John 14.

Line 15: 'in illo acquirit salutem in quo solo homo invenerit innocentem' is obscure; perhaps 'in whom alone it has found man innocent'. Line 16: the edition cites Ps. 148:6; the quoted words are 148:5. Line 21 'percurremus' read as 'percurrimus'. Line 23: the sentence 'Quo ... peregrinum' is awkward and possibly corrupt; rendered tentatively.

Line 4 opening ("fides vestra non admonet religionis promere documenta") is elliptical; the sense "your faith does not require us to set forth" is a guess. Line 10: the edition suggests reading appenderetur or penderet for penderetur, and manentibus ("remaining") for morientibus ("dying"); "eternal [death]" supplies an evident ellipsis. Line 14: the editor suspects esse is missing ("[that we are] from God"); 'osus' read as ejus.

Sermon VII closely follows Melito of Sardis' homily On the Pascha (Peri Pascha), in a Latin version; the editors do not mention this. Line 33: 'comminutus' (broken) may render Greek 'slain/broken up'; kept literally. Line 34: 'velut ab Ægypto nos a mundi cultura' read as 'from the worship (cultura) of the world'. Line 35: 'gulis' read as 'funibus/vinculis' sense (cords), probably for 'funibus' or 'vinculis'; 'opulis' taken as 'epulis' (rich food), 'esunem' as 'esuriem'; 'Non es inter opera ejus' is obscure, perhaps corrupt for 'Non es veritus opera ejus' (you did not respect his works). Line 36: 'Ego resuscitabo' lacks an object; 'you' supplied. Line 37: 'tegendi' read as 'legendi' (reading), as the rest of the admonition requires; 'Hitorpio' = Melchior Hittorp, 'Frontone' = Fronton du Duc or Jean Fronteau (uncertain).

Sermon IX, ch. 3: 'dies perfici meruerunt' is translated as 'deserved to be made day', taking it as 'dies effici'; the transmitted wording is awkward. The verse cited as Ps. 77:65 is given as the text has it ('Resurrexit'); the Vulgate reads 'Excitatus est'. In ch. 1, 'jungebatur Verbo' apparently refers to the Incarnation at the Annunciation.

In Sermon X, ch. 2, 'Quantumvis blanditur mundus, habet delectationem illam' is elliptical; the subject of 'habet' is taken as God (the delight 'in your right hand'), marked with [God]. In Sermon X, ch. 1, 'in insto initio' is read as 'in isto initio'. In Sermon XI, ch. 3, 'sitientes' is translated with the edition's alternative 'sentientes' given in brackets as printed. 'Erigate' in Sermon IX, ch. 4 is read as 'erogate'.

Sermon XII: the text is cut short; the editors note the end seems missing. Chap. IV: the sentence 'Sed ubi desiderium ... intelligit, ac blandiori cum requie confoveri' lacks a main verb (probably 'jubet' or similar has dropped out); '[he orders him]' is supplied. Chap. V: 'contenta persecutor' presumably for 'contenta persecutorem'; translated so. The Lord's 'domum horreis' read as 'Domini horreis'. Footnote letters (a)–(k) omitted.

Line 60: 'mentorum' is probably a scanning error, perhaps for 'meritorum' (merits); rendered so, but uncertain. 'derox' read as 'ferox'. Line 63: the sentence 'Si enim tunc temporis ... agebatur in Galliis jampridem dubio procul ... debueret' appears to lack words (a 'quin' or similar) but the sense is clear. The list cited from Boucher gives 'VIII kal. Februarii', apparently in conflict with the following argument for 'VIII kal. Martii'; possibly an error in the text. Quesnel's 'VIII kal. Martii' and the editors' closing 'VII kal. Martii' for Sylvius' calendar also differ; translated as given.

Editorial footnote marks (a)-(g) omitted. Ch. VI: the saying 'We cannot rejoice here with the world and reign there with the Lord' is attributed to Paul but is not found in Scripture; the following quotation is from Acts (spoken by Paul and Barnabas). Ch. IV: the Psalm quotation reads 'Dominum' where the Psalm has 'eum'; 'Si namque... fundata' is grammatically incomplete in the Latin and has been rendered as a statement.

Line 70: 'prædicante [forte præstante]' is the edition's own conjecture ('perhaps granting'); a stray 'Amen' before 'Christo' is omitted. Matt. reference printed as XIX, 23 (properly 19:28). Line 73: 'quæ maternum non succum' lacks a verb ('habeo' supplied); 'angeli præsentiam fortius notare' is syntactically incomplete; 'Priusquam angelus ... susciperet' is obscure and rendered loosely. Line 74: 'Intemeritas servatur virginitates... naturæ' seems corrupt (read 'intemerata ... virginitas'); 'Duc' read as 'Dic', 'ca-tum' as 'castum', 'huhumilem' as 'ad humilem'. The mundus/mundum wordplay (world/clean) cannot be kept in English. 'sedens super nebulam' (on a cloud) stands for the ass of Zech. 9:9 in this text; 'sine compari sidere' is obscure.

Line 75: 'Ita (a) praesumptis passiones paralytici' is corrupt (the edition's note mark suggests a problem); rendered by conjecture as 'So too [he took on] the sufferings of the paralytic'. 'exeuntem de servitute' is obscure. 'acrem' read as 'aerem'. Line 79: 'Unus ex rustico insertus' seems corrupt; rendered literally. 'apostolorum' read as 'apostolatum'; 'coronaverunt' rendered by the edition's suggested 'cucurrerunt'. Line 80: 'mossa' read as 'missa'. Line 81: 'ibid quod' read as 'ob id quod'/'eo quod'; 'duantocius' as 'quantocius'.

Line 82–84: obvious scanning errors read as intended (e.g. turia = furia, linganimitatis = longanimitatis, culorem = cultorem, terium usque ... cælum = tertium usque cælum, dedidi = dediti). In 83, 'Paulum enim percussit' may be a corruption of 'paululum' ('he struck him a little'), which would match the preceding 'modicum'. Line 85 'A' is a stray column/page marker from the printed edition, kept as it stands. Line 86: 'Nec mirum sane si sancto Petro porta jam in potestatem acceperat' is evidently corrupt (the following clause's words repeated); rendered by sense as '[opened]'. Line 87: 'Sec nec aliter de carcere. in est' read as 'Sed nec aliter de carcere, id est'; 'circulo' kept, with the edition's suggestion 'cingulo' (girdle) in view; the 'Apostle' quotation is actually Luke 12:35.

Footnote letters of the printed page have been omitted. Obvious misprints read as: 'Liberii' for 'Liberti', 'Carolum' for 'Coralum', 'Adrianus' for 'Andrianus', 'collocatus' for 'collocutus', 'demonstraverimus' for 'demonstravimus', 'Gelasiano' for 'Gelasiako'. In line 90 the edition numbers two points '5°'; the first is rendered as 4th. 'Monsacratus' is taken to be the abbot Monsacrati; 'pagina 1' in line 92 may be a footnote mark rather than a page reference.

Line 99: text is lost between 'infir-' and 'indissolubilem' (a line of the printed page seems dropped; probably 'infirmum ... per'), marked [...]. Line 102: the reference 'Joan. XIII, 17' is a misprint for John 8:17. Line 103: in the Sedulius quotation 'stane lumine vitae' is read as 'sine lumine vitae'. In line 102, 'castum veterem casto novo' could also be taken as 'the old chaste man to the new chaste man' in the reverse direction; the sense pairs Elijah with John.

The text ends abruptly at 'per num', evidently a garbled form of the closing doxology 'per omnia saecula saeculorum'; the ending is supplied in brackets. Several scanning errors (Dertas for Deitas, cognoscir for cognosci, auox for quos, luvem for lucem, cim for cum, sanvto for sancto) are read as evident.

nodes.text: SERMONS ATTRIBUTED TO ST LEO THE GREAT.
ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING TRACTATE.

This tractate was first edited from Vatican codex 2346 by Gerard Vossius of Tongeren, and inserted among the Miscellanea of several holy Fathers appended to the edition of St Gregory Thaumaturgus (Mainz, 1604); thereafter it found a place in other editions of St Leo. Vossius noted, however, that in that manuscript it bears this less fitting title: Leo, pope, bishop of the first see, to Flavian, on the errors of Eutyches; just as if it were the very letter addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. We found the same tractate in another codex, Vatican Queen of Sweden 139, of about the fourteenth century, which contains the Works of Leo. Its heading there, on page 460, is this: The Faith of Pope Leo, which St Gregory wonderfully praises in his letters, saying thus: "Whoever adds to or takes from the faith of St Leo the pope, or does not embrace it fully down to the smallest atom, is in no way to be called a bishop, but is to be struck with anathema." St Gregory, however, wrote this not of this tractate but of the celebrated letter to Flavian. Likewise, after the tractate this annotation is placed in the same codex: The canons prescribe that in the first synod the letters of blessed Pope Leo, which he wrote to Flavian on the error of Eutyches, be read. We also came upon the same tractate in Vatican manuscript 551, which will be seen to differ from Vossius' codex from a number of variants, and especially from the final note. The codex is of about the twelfth century and contains the Letters of Jerome, before which this tractate is placed with this title: Leo, pope, bishop of the first see, to (with "Flavian" added by a later hand), where the writing of the first hand had been erased. Afterwards this note is appended: This is that faith which St Gregory, etc., and then: The canons prescribe, etc., as in the Vatican Queen's codex.

Quesnel believed that this tractate should be relegated to the appendix as certainly spurious, on the ground that he took it for a cento stitched together from Leo's writings. For everything in it is taken from here and there, copied word for word from various texts of the holy pontiff, now from the Sermons, now from the Letters, as is indicated in the margin. Vossius, after indicating the sources from which this tractate was put together, adds this: We have decided to adduce here these passages which we have compared, if only so that it may be clear that this is the true teaching of St Leo. But whether the present tractate was composed in this form by St Leo himself, or was made up by others from his teaching, does not seem worth investigating closely here. One thing at least we know for certain from the Letters of St Leo, that the same things are often repeated in one letter after another. But the falseness of the title first raises suspicion; then difficulty is caused by a number of passages which appear to give the reason for what precedes, yet do not cohere well enough with what precedes, as will become especially clear from note 38. We therefore believe there can be no doubt that it is a cento, which someone put together without much skill; and accordingly we have thought that this tractate should be left in the appendix into which Quesnel had thrown it. We have, however, given the first place to this cento, because works of this kind are of a middle status between the genuine and the spurious; for what consists of Leo's own words and thoughts is not wholly foreign to him, nor again is it wholly his own, since it was arranged by another. Although Vossius used only one codex in editing this tractate, he nevertheless noted some variants in the margin, which he took from the reading of the Sermons or Letters, and later editions present only these. We shall add others from the two manuscripts cited just above, the Vatican and the Queen's, or, where it is appropriate, we shall transfer them into the text, indicating the old reading.
881 SERMON I.
Or Tractate against the errors of Eutyches and other heretics.

CHAP. I. — For the instruction of the sons of the Church, the service of our discourse must be added. For we do not fear that the spiritual and learned will disdain what they know, since it belongs to their fruitfulness to impart to others what they themselves have learned to their own great profit. So let the dispensing of divine gifts take place through the hearts of all, and let the learned and unlearned not spurn the service of our mouth. May the bounty of him of whose majesty we attempt to speak also aid our faith, so that for the advancement of his whole Church he may make both you able to receive and us abundant [in giving]. When, therefore, we direct the eyes of the mind to understanding the dignity of the Holy Spirit, let us think nothing different from the excellence of the Father and the Son, because the essence of the divine Trinity in no respect departs from its unity. It is eternal for the Father to be the begetter of a Son coeternal with himself. It is eternal for the Son to have been begotten of the Father outside time. It is eternal also for the Holy Spirit to be the Spirit of the Father and the Son: so that the Father was never without the Son, the Son never without the Father, the Father and the Son never without the Holy Spirit; and, all degrees of existence being excluded, no person there is earlier, none later. For the unchangeable Godhead of this blessed Trinity is one in substance, undivided in work, sharing in will, equal in omnipotence, equal in glory. When holy Scripture speaks of it in such a way as to designate, whether in deeds or in words, something that seems to befit individual persons, the catholic faith is not disturbed but instructed: so that through what is proper either to a word or to a work the truth of the Trinity may be conveyed to us, and the understanding may not divide what the hearing distinguishes. For this is why certain things are set forth under the name either of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, that the confession of the faithful may not err concerning the Trinity. Since it is inseparable, it would never be understood to be a Trinity if it were always spoken of inseparably. Well, then, does the very difficulty of speaking draw our heart 396 to understanding, and the heavenly teaching helps us through our weakness: so that, since in the Godhead of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit neither singleness nor diversity is to be conceived, true unity and true Trinity can indeed be perceived together by the mind, but cannot be uttered together by the mouth. With this faith, then, dearly beloved, founded in our hearts, we believe to our salvation that the whole Trinity together is one power, one majesty, one substance, undivided in operation, inseparable in love, undifferentiated in might, together filling all things, together containing the universe. For what the Father is, this the Son is also, this the Holy Spirit is also; and true Godhead cannot in any respect be either less or greater. It is to be so confessed in three persons that the Trinity does not admit solitude, and equality preserves unity.

CHAP. II. — For the majesty of the Holy Spirit is never separated from the omnipotence of the Father and the Son. And whatever the divine governance does in the ordering of all things comes from the providence of the whole Trinity. There is one kindness of mercy there, one judgement of justice; nor is anything divided in action where nothing is different in will. What the Father illuminates, then, the Son illuminates, the Holy Spirit illuminates. And since the person of the one sent is one, that of the sender another, that of the one promising another, both unity and Trinity are shown to us together; so that the essence, having equality and not admitting solitude, is understood to be both of the same substance and not of the same person. That, then, while the cooperation of the inseparable Godhead is preserved, the Father carries out certain things, the Son certain things, the Holy Spirit certain things properly, is the plan of our redemption, the ordering of our salvation. For if man, made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1), had remained in the honour of his nature, and had not, deceived by the devil's fraud, strayed through concupiscence from the law laid down for him, the creator of the world would not have become a creature: nor would the eternal have undergone temporality, or God the Son, equal to God the Father, have taken the form of a servant and the likeness of sinful flesh. But since through the envy of the devil death entered into the world (Wis. 2), and human captivity could not be loosed otherwise than if he took up our cause without loss to his majesty, and 887 became true man, and alone had no contagion of sin: the mercy of the Trinity divided among itself the work of our restoration, so that the Father should be propitiated, the Son should propitiate, the Holy Spirit should kindle. If, therefore, dearly beloved, with grace as our guide, we come to know faithfully and wisely what is proper to the Father, what to the Son, what to the Holy Spirit in our restoration, or what is common, we shall without doubt so receive the things done for us in humility and in the body that we think nothing unworthy of the one and same glory of the Trinity. For although no mind is adequate to thinking of God, no tongue to speaking [of him], yet whatever that may be which is reached by human understanding concerning the essence of the Father's Godhead, unless it is one and the same when one thinks either of his Only-begotten or of the Holy Spirit, it is not piously understood but darkened in too carnal a fashion, and even what seemed to be fittingly thought of the Father is lost: because one departs from the whole Trinity if unity is not held in it. But in no way is that truly one which is diverse through any inequality. When, therefore, we direct the gaze of the mind to confessing the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, let us drive far from the mind the forms of visible things and the ages of temporal natures, far the bodies of places and the places of bodies. Let there depart from the heart what is extended in space, what is enclosed by a limit, and whatever is neither always, nor everywhere, nor whole. Let thought conceived about the Godhead of the Trinity understand nothing through distance, seek nothing through degrees; or, if it has perceived anything worthy of God, let it not dare to deny this there to any person.

CHAP. III. — This faith, however, earthly wisdom did not discover, nor did human opinion persuade [us of it]; but the only-begotten Son himself taught it, the Holy Spirit himself established it: concerning whom nothing is to be thought otherwise than concerning the Father and the Son: because although he is not the Father, is not the Son, he is nevertheless not divided from the Father and the Son. And just as he has his own person in the Trinity, so he has one substance in the Godhead of the Father and the Son, filling all things, containing all things, and with the Father and the Son governing the universe for ever. For what is so opposed to the prophets, so contrary to the Gospels, so rebellious, in short, against the apostolic teachings, as to preach one single nature in the Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary and timelessly co-eternal with the everlasting Father? For if it is to be understood as of man only, where is the Godhead that saves? If only 398 of God, where is the humanity that is saved? But the catholic faith, which resists all errors, refutes these impieties also at once, condemning Nestorius, who divides the divine from the human, and abhorring Eutyches, who empties the human in the divine: since the Son of the true God, true God, having unity and equality with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, deigned also to be true man, separated from the flesh neither in the conception by the virgin mother nor in the birth: so uniting humanity to himself that he remained unchangeably God; so imparting Godhead to the man that he did not consume him by glorification but increased him. For he who was made in the form of a servant did not cease to be in the form of God; nor is he one thing in the one and another in the other, but he is one in both. Let our faith be disturbed by no varieties of [his] dispensations, but whether in miracles of power or in the insults of the passion, let us believe both that he who is man is God, and that he who is God is man. Thus the one Christ is true God and true man, rich in what is his own, poor in what is ours; receiving gifts and pouring out gifts; sharer with mortals and the bringing to life of the dead: so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bend.

CHAP. IV. — If, then, Eutyches did not know what he ought to think about the incarnation of the Word of God, and was unwilling to labour over the breadth of the holy Scriptures, he should at least have received with attentive hearing that common confession by which the whole body of the faithful professes that it believes in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his only Son our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and [born of] the Virgin Mary. By these three statements the devices of almost all heretics are destroyed. For when God is believed to be also almighty Father, the Son is shown to be everlasting with him, differing from the Father in nothing: because he was born God from God, almighty from almighty, co-eternal from the eternal: not later in time, not inferior in power, not unlike in glory, not divided in essence. And the same everlasting Only-begotten of the everlasting Begetter was born of the Holy Spirit, from the Virgin Mary. This temporal birth took nothing away from that divine and everlasting birth, and added nothing to it; but spent itself wholly on restoring man, who had been deceived, both that it might conquer death and by its power destroy the devil, who had the dominion of death.

CHAP. V. — In this conflict too, entered upon for us, the contest was waged by a great and wonderful law of equity, while almighty God engages the most savage enemy not in his own majesty but in 398 our lowliness, setting against him the same form and the same nature, sharing indeed in our mortality but free of all sin. For we could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he took up our nature and made it his own, whom neither sin could defile nor death hold fast. For he was conceived by the Holy Spirit within the womb of the Virgin mother, who bore him with her virginity intact, just as with her virginity intact she conceived [him]. Or did that heretic perhaps think that our Lord Jesus Christ was not of our nature because the angel sent to the Virgin said: And the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and therefore also the holy thing that will be born of you will be called the Son of God (Luke 1): as though, because the Virgin's conception was a divine work, the flesh of the one conceived was not of the nature of her who conceived? But that generation, singularly wonderful and wonderfully singular, is not to be understood in such a way that by the novelty of the creation the property of the kind was removed. For the Holy Spirit gave fruitfulness to the Virgin, but the reality of the body was taken from a body; and as Wisdom built herself a house (Prov. 9), the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1), that is, in that flesh which he took from man and which the spirit of rational life animated. Therefore the Word of God, God, the Son of God, who in the beginning was with God, through whom all things were made, without whom nothing was made, became man in order to free man from eternal death, so bending himself to take up our lowliness without diminution of his majesty that, remaining what he was and assuming what he was not, he united the true form of a servant to that form in which he is equal to God the Father, and joined both natures in so great a bond that neither did glorification consume the lower nor assumption diminish the higher.

CHAP. VI. — The property of each nature, therefore, being preserved and coming together into one person, lowliness was taken up by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity; and to pay off the debt of our condition the inviolable nature was united to the passible nature, so that, as suited our remedy, one and the same mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, could both die by the one and not die by the other. In the complete perfection, then, of true man and of [his] true nature, true God was born, 400 whole in what is his own and whole in what is ours. By 'ours' we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and what he took up to restore. For those things which the deceiver brought in and man, deceived, admitted had no trace in the Saviour. Nor, because he underwent the fellowship of human weaknesses, was he therefore a sharer in our sins. He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, increasing the human, not diminishing the divine, because that emptying by which the invisible showed himself visible, and the Creator and Lord of all things willed to be one of mortals, was a stooping of compassion, not a failure of power. Accordingly, he who, remaining in the form of God, made man, the same in the form of a servant was made man. For each nature keeps its own property without loss. And just as the form of a servant does not take away the form of God, so the form of God does not diminish the form of a servant. For since the devil boasted that man, deceived by his fraud, had lost the divine gifts and, stripped of the dowry of immortality, had undergone the harsh sentence of death, and that he had found in his own evils some consolation from the fellowship of a transgressor, and that God too, as the principle of justice demanded, had changed his own purpose towards man, whom he had created in such honour: there was need of a dispensation of secret counsel, so that the unchangeable God (whose will cannot be deprived of its kindness) might fulfil by a more hidden mystery the first dispensation of his loving-kindness towards us, and that man, driven into guilt by the cunning of diabolical wickedness, might not perish contrary to God's purpose.

CHAP. VII. — The Son of God therefore enters these weak places of the world, descending from his heavenly seat yet not departing from the Father's glory, begotten in a new order, by a new birth. In a new order, because, invisible in what is his own, he became visible in what is ours. The incomprehensible willed to be comprehended. Abiding before times, he began to exist in time. The Lord of the universe took up the form of a servant, the immensity of his majesty overshadowed. The impassible God did not disdain to be passible man, and, immortal, to submit to the laws of death. And begotten by a new birth, because inviolate virginity, which knew no concupiscence, supplied the matter of the flesh. From the mother of the Lord nature was assumed, not guilt; nor, in the Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin's womb, is [his nature], because the birth is wonderful, therefore unlike our nature. 401 For he who is true God is the same who is true man. And there is no falsehood in this unity, since the lowliness of man and the loftiness of the Godhead are mutually [in each other]. For as God is not changed by compassion, so man is not consumed by dignity: for each form does what is proper to it in communion with the other, the Word, that is, performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines with miracles, the other succumbs to injuries. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the Father's glory, so the flesh has not abandoned the nature of our race. For one and the same is — as must often be said — truly Son of God and truly Son of man: God by virtue of the fact that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; man by virtue of the fact that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1). Him whom, as a man, diabolical cunning tempts, the same, as God, angelic services wait upon. To hunger, to thirst, to grow weary and to sleep is evidently human. But to satisfy five thousand men with five loaves, to bestow on the Samaritan woman living water, the drinking of which grants the drinker that he thirst no more, to walk on the back of the sea with feet that do not sink, and to level the swelling of the waves by rebuking the storm, is without ambiguity divine. Just as, then (to pass over many things), it is not of the same nature to weep with the feeling of compassion for Lazarus, a dead friend, and, when the mound of the four-days' burial had been removed, to raise the same man to life again at the command of his voice; or to hang on the cross and, daylight turned to night, to make all the elements tremble; or to be pierced with nails and to open the gate of paradise to the faith of the thief: so it is not of the same nature to say: I and the Father are one (John 10); and to say: The Father is greater than I (ibid. 14). For although in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and man, yet the source from which the insult is common to both is one thing, and the source from which the glory is common is another. For from what is ours he has a humanity less than the Father; from the Father he has a Godhead equal with the Father.

CHAP. VIII. Therefore, because of this unity of person, which is to be understood in both natures, the Son of man too is read to have come down from heaven, since the Son of God took flesh from that Virgin of whom he was born. And again the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, since he suffered these things not in the Godhead itself, in which as Only-begotten he is co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father, but in the weakness of human nature. Hence we all confess in the Creed also that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, according to that saying of the Apostle: For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty (1 Cor. 2). For the Catholic Church lives by this faith and advances by it, that in the Lord Jesus Christ neither is the humanity believed to be without true Godhead, nor the Godhead without true humanity. But when Eutyches professed in the Council that our Lord was of two natures before the union, but confessed one nature after the union, I am amazed that so absurd and so perverse a profession of his was not checked by any rebuke from the judges, and that a speech so very foolish and so very blasphemous was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard. For it is as impious to say that the Only-begotten Son of God was of two natures before the incarnation as it is wicked to assert that, after the Word was made flesh, there is a single nature in him. Let not Eutyches think this was said either rightly or tolerably because it was refuted by no verdict. For the true faith is defended most fruitfully when a false opinion is condemned even by its own followers.

CHAP. IX. Amid these things, then, as far as Nestorius strayed from the truth by separating the Godhead of the Word from the substance of the man assumed, so far did this man also depart from the right path, who proclaims that the only-begotten Son of God was so born from the womb of the blessed Virgin that he bore indeed the appearance of a human body, but the reality of human flesh was not united to the Word. Who does not see what monstrous opinions are born from this prodigy of falsehood? For [if the nature] of the mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, is denied, he must be filled with many impieties, and either Apollinaris claims him for himself, or Valentinus seizes him, or Manichaeus holds him, none of whom believed in the reality of human flesh in Christ Jesus. And if this is not accepted, not only is it denied that he who was in the form of God, remaining the same in the form of a servant, was born a man according to flesh and rational soul, but it is also refused that he was crucified and died and was buried, and that on the third day he rose from the dead, and that, sitting at the right hand of God the Father, he will come to judge the living and the dead in that body in which he was judged. For these mysteries of our redemption are emptied if Christ is not believed to have taken the true and whole nature of a true man. Or, because the divine signs were manifest, shall the bodily proofs be called false? And shall the testimonies of both natures avail for the Creator to be recognised, but not avail for the creature to be saved? What belongs to the Godhead the flesh does not diminish; what belongs to the flesh the Godhead does not destroy. For the same one is both eternal from the Father and temporal from the mother: inviolable in his own power, passible in our weakness; in the Godhead of the Trinity of one and the same nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but in the taking up of man not of one substance but of one and the same person; so that the same one might be rich in poverty, almighty in abasement, impassible in punishment, immortal in death. For the Word was not changed in any part of itself into either flesh or soul, since the simple and unchangeable nature of the Godhead is always whole in its own essence, receiving neither loss nor increase of itself, and so blessing the nature assumed that, glorified, it remains in him who glorifies [it]. And why should it seem unfitting or impossible that the Word and flesh and soul should be one Jesus Christ and one Son of God and man, if flesh and soul, which are of unlike natures, make one person even without the incarnation of the Word, since it is much easier for the power of the Godhead to bring about this unity of itself and man than for the weakness of humanity alone to achieve it in its own substances? So neither was the Word changed into flesh, nor the flesh into the Word, but both remain in one, and one is in both, not divided by diversity nor confounded by mixture. Nor is he one from the Father and another from the mother, but the same, in one way from the Father before every beginning, in another way from the mother at the end of the ages; so that he might be the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2), in whom the fullness of the Godhead should dwell bodily (Col. 2). For it is the advancement of the one assumed, not of the one assuming, that God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name (Phil. 2).

CHAP. X. For the birth of the Lord according to the flesh, although it has certain properties by which it transcends the beginnings of the human condition, whether because he alone was conceived and born of an inviolate Virgin without concupiscence of the flesh, or because he was brought forth from his mother's womb in such a way that fruitfulness gave birth and virginity remained, yet his flesh was not of another nature [than] ours, nor was the soul breathed into him from another principle than into other men, a soul which excelled not by diversity of kind but by loftiness of virtue. For he had nothing opposed to his flesh, nor did discord of desires produce a conflict of wills. The bodily senses were vigorous without the law of sin, and the reality of the affections, under the governance of the Godhead and the mind, was neither tempted by allurements nor yielded to injuries. True man was united to true God; he was neither brought down from heaven as to a pre-existing soul, nor created out of nothing as to the flesh, bearing the same person in the Godhead of the Word, and holding a nature common with us in body and soul. For he would not be the mediator between God and men unless the same, God and man, were in both both one and true. Next, we do not call Christ God only, as the Manichaean heretics do, nor man only, as the Photinian heretics do; nor man in such a way that anything is lacking to him which certainly belongs to human nature, whether soul, or rational mind, or flesh, as though it were not taken from a woman but made from the Word, converted and changed into flesh: these three false and empty [opinions] of the Apollinarian heretics produced three different factions. Nor do we say that the blessed Virgin Mary conceived a man without Godhead, who, created by the Holy Spirit, was afterwards taken up by the Word, which we rightly and justly condemned when Nestorius preached it; but we say that Christ the Son of God, true God, was born of God the Father without any beginning of time, and that the same, true man, was born of a human mother in the fixed fullness of time; and that his humanity, by which the Father is greater, does not diminish anything of that nature of his which is equal to the Father. And both of these are one Christ, who said most truly, both according to God: I and the Father are one (John 10); and according to man: The Father is greater than I (John 14).

CHAP. XI. Although, then, in our one Lord Jesus Christ, true Son of God and man, there is one person of the Word and the flesh, and both essences have their actions in common, yet the qualities of the works themselves are to be understood, and by the contemplation of sincere faith it must be discerned to what the lowliness of weakness is raised, and to what the height of power stoops: what it is that the flesh does not do without the Word, and what it is that the Word does not accomplish without the flesh. For without the power of the Word the virgin would not conceive nor bear, and without the reality of the flesh the infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not lie [in the manger]. Without the power of the Word there would be no restoring of the infirm and no bringing to life of the dead, and without the reality of the flesh neither would food be needed by the fasting nor sleep by the weary. Lastly, without the power of the Word the Lord would not profess himself equal to the Father, and without the reality of the flesh the same would not say that the Father is greater, since the Catholic faith accepts both and defends both, believing, according to the property of the divine and human substance, one Son of God both man and Word. Although, therefore, from that beginning when in the virgin's womb the Word was made flesh (John 1) there has never been any division between the divine and human substance, and through all the bodily growth the actions of all that time were those of one person, yet we do not confound by any mixture those very things which were done inseparably, but we perceive from the quality of the works what belongs to each form. Neither do the divine things prejudice the human, nor the human the divine, since both so meet in one and the same that in them neither is the property consumed nor the person doubled. Although, then, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and in him there is altogether one and the same person of true Godhead and true humanity, and the solidity of this union can be severed by no division, yet the exaltation, in that God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, we understand to belong to that form which was to be enriched by the increase of so great a glorification. For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the begetter and the only-begotten there was no distinction in essence, no difference in majesty; nor through the mystery of the incarnation had anything departed from the Word which would be restored by the gift of God the Father. But the form of a servant, through which the impassible Godhead fulfilled the mystery of great loving-kindness, is human lowliness, which by the glory of divine power was raised into so great a unity, Godhead and humanity being joined from the very conception by the virgin, that neither were divine things done without man nor human things without God. For this reason, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who from eternity is equal to God is said to have been exalted. Nor does it matter from which substance Christ is named, since, the unity of the person remaining inseparable, the same is both wholly son of man on account of the flesh and wholly Son of God on account of the one Godhead with the Father. Whatever, then, Christ received in time, he received according to man, to whom the things he did not have are conferred. For according to the power of the Word the Son too has, without difference, all things that the Father has; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, the same he himself also gave in the form of the Father.

CHAP. XII. — This faith, though very many heretics have attacked it, Nestorius and Eutyches, with different assertions indeed but with like impiety, have tried to break into. Let Nestorius therefore be anathematized, who believed the blessed Virgin to be the mother of a man only, so as to make one person of the flesh and another of the Godhead; whereas within the virgin's womb the Word was made flesh in such a way that, through an ineffable mystery, by one conception and one birth, according to the truth and union of both natures, the same virgin was both handmaid of the Lord and mother. Let Eutyches also be struck with the same anathema, who, denying the reality of human flesh and soul, asserted that our whole Lord Jesus Christ is of one nature, as though the Godhead of the Word had itself converted itself into flesh and soul. These lies, so sacrilegious, have been condemned throughout the whole world by the judgements of the holy Fathers. But the catholic faith, unique and true, which justifies the ungodly and creates the just, being drawn to share in his humanity, acquires salvation in him in whom alone man has found [himself] innocent. This faith, according to the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic teaching and that of the saving creed, the Synod of Nicaea established, the examination at Chalcedon confirmed, and the whole world celebrates and venerates. This same [faith], dearly beloved, defend with a devout and praiseworthy love, or rather hold it faithfully and firmly, and assert it constantly. For, as the blessed apostle Paul says, great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the gentiles, was believed in this world, was taken up in glory (1 Tim. 3:16).
SERMON II.
On the Nativity of the Lord.
Published in Quesnel's appendix from the codex of St Peter of Corbie, in which it is attributed to St Leo.

CHAP. I. — Our Saviour, dearly beloved, is born today; let us rejoice: for there ought to be no place for sadness where there is the birthday of joys. This joy, then, belongs to all, because Christ came for all. Let no one, therefore, think himself a stranger to the gladness of this day. If anyone is holy, let him rejoice, because he will receive a reward. If he is a sinner, let him rejoice, because he is invited to pardon. If he is a gentile, let him rejoice, because he is admitted to salvation. God took on the flesh of the human race for us. If we do not make ourselves strangers to Christ, we are already in Christ. Let us recognize, then, our redemption; let us recognize our salvation. He makes himself a stranger to fellowship with Christ who denies that he is in the body of Christ. But since, dearly beloved, according to the Scriptures which have been read, we know that the Lord was born today, let us see how he was born at the end of the age who is the creator of the ages: for he spoke and they were made; he commanded and they were created (Ps. 148:5).

CHAP. II. — Christ our Saviour, then, dearly beloved, is believed to be man and God: God from the Father, man from the mother; God from the Godhead, bodily from the flesh; and therefore God before the ages, man after the ages; God before the beginnings, man among the last things, who in the beginning created through his majesty, [and] today came to save through the flesh. The creation of men was the first [act of] power; salvation the second [act of] loving-kindness. Moved by the affection of kindness, the Lord willed to restore to us by mercy whatever offence had taken away. He descended, therefore, that we might ascend; he lowered heavenly things to raise up earthly ones; he made himself a sharer in man to make man a partaker of God; made, as you have heard through the Apostle, made of a woman, made under the law (Gal. 4:4). But let no one, when he hears that the mother of the Lord was a woman, be disturbed by offence at the name. A virgin conceived of the Holy Spirit, but she is called a woman from her sex. And therefore the evangelist who was read called her a virgin, but the apostle a woman: so that all might recognize the omnipotence of the Godhead in the Virgin's childbearing, and in the name 'woman' hear the name of [her] condition.

CHAP. III. — Our Lord, then, was born of flesh indeed, but not of carnal corruption; born as a man, but not begotten as a man. He took up flesh in such a way as to preserve the honour of majesty. And thus, separating the purity of his birth from contact with human defilement, he accomplished in his birth the full dispensation of a man, yet did not abandon the dignity of God. And so in this world, such as he was in his birth, he kept the purity of his origin also in the integrity of his life. For he alone is the one in whose mouth, as it is written, there was no deceit: so that he who had not known human defilement in his creation should not know it in his manner of life either. For, says the Apostle, though he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant, etc. All men, dearly beloved, were servants of sins, and therefore the Apostle rightly says that he assumed only the form of a servant, because, being true man but not defiled by human vices, he had only the form of a servant, not its conscience: because though he had the appearance of a man, yet he had not the conscience of a sinner: because, as the Apostle says, Though he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2:6). A man in appearance, but God in power; a servant as it were in form, but Lord in nature: outwardly showing the weakness of his mother, inwardly possessing the majesty of the Father; outwardly lowly in body, inwardly mighty in Godhead.

CHAP. IV. — Finally, his very manner of life among men showed both at once: man in his sufferings, God in his miracles. For he hungered, but he fed the hungry with loaves multiplied through blessing. That he hungered was the flesh; that he fed [them] was God. It was from the man that he wept; from the Godhead that he bestowed. It showed the man that he poured out prayer, prayed, and was heard. In all things, then, he showed a twofold nature in himself, and therefore he is mediator of both substances: because while he lowered heavenly things, he exalted human ones: he made the highest harmony out of diversity, so that both became one in him who holds both in himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON III.
On Lent I.

Now first published from three codices, the Venetian of St Mark 153, the Paduan of the Eremitan Fathers 113, and the Veronese 214, in which it is attributed to Pope St Leo; but by the marks set out in the preface, no. 4, another unknown ancient author is revealed. Aeneas of Paris, who quotes no small part of this sermon in his book against the Greeks (vol. I of the Spicilegium of Achery), assigns it to St Faustinus the bishop, to whom other

sermons too are ascribed in some manuscripts, as the Benedictine Fathers noted in the appendix to vol. V of the Works of St Augustine. In the Paduan codex it is headed, Sunday, beginning of Lent; and that this sermon was delivered on the first Sunday of Lent is clear from the beginning of chapters 1 and 3.

CHAP. I. — I believe you have been puzzled, dearest brothers, why we have been running through Lent from the previous Sunday, and, since this day is its beginning, why we began to celebrate its festival a week earlier. This observance cannot be blamed: for it is a sign of the very best devotion to carry out the law before you know the law's statutes, and to obey the commands before the commands compel obedience. The one belongs to love, the other to fear. The latter is exacted by command, the former is offered out of piety. In the one a debt is paid, in the other the gift of a present is displayed. Hence we too have offered a pious gift to God, in fasting more. For a festival hastened cannot be blamed. For in joys our prayers always anticipate the solemnity, and devotion, while it longs for future gladness, anticipates it. Not only, then, was it done without blame, but also with caution. For in doubtful matters one should always add something more for caution's sake, because what is more can be cut back, but what is less cannot be extended, as was done in this observance. For in fasting more on account of Lent we have not diminished Lent: it remains whole for us. But if we had fasted less than the number, we could not have restored it to the number.

CHAP. II. — But perhaps the point at issue is that the fasting we have done does not count for us toward Lent. It plainly profits us, because even if it does not count toward Lent, it profits toward salvation. If it does not count toward the number, it profits toward merit. For whom has it ever not profited to pray, to read, to fast? Whom have chastity, sobriety, gentleness not profited? Except that I think those more to be blamed who, though they had been ready to fast, after they heard that the solemnities were doubtful, neglected to fast. They showed indeed that they wished to live piously not willingly but under compulsion. They feared, I suppose, that if the fasts were prolonged by five days their flesh and body would fail them, and that, thin and weak, they would not be able to endure the abstinence of Lent.

CHAP. III. — Let them hear, then, both the well-fed and the robust, and the thin and pale, that today is Lent. Let the former hear, I say, so that they may begin to fast; and the latter, so that they may not cease to abstain, and that together they may hasten to enter the ark of Christ. Indeed, let those hasten all the more who began to abstain later, so that they may enter more chastened and purer. For the ark of the Lord is able to support fasting in dangers; it does not know how to bear the drunken. We therefore admonish you, as we have said before, men of our time, that in the whirlwinds of this world each one should eagerly take refuge in the house of God, just as Noah the just admonished the men of his time. For he warned them of the coming flood, and did not cease to preach; and though the voice of his preaching was not heard, yet even if his tongue was silent, his works spoke; even if words were silent, the construction resounded. For when he was building so great a work as that ark, he bore witness by the work itself to the reason why it was being made. For by the very preparation he testified that new dwellings would serve against new dangers. For any wise man could understand that some shipwreck or other was impending, when a house of such a kind was being made as would not cling to the earth but float on the deep; when a lodging of this sort was being prepared that would neither fix its floor on the ground nor be submerged by the waves. Who, I say, being wise, would not understand that a flood was at hand, when he saw such a dwelling being made as would not so much enclose those received within it as carry them, and would not so much keep off showers of rain as ward off the storms of shipwreck? From what lodging, I say, would he not perceive man's danger: a lodging in which one would not be dwelling but rather living in exile; in whatever part of the world it should be, the dwelling with them would be a wanderer's. So holy Noah himself preached to the peoples by his work, and spoke that saying of the Lord in the Gospel: If you do not believe me, believe the works (John 10:38).
SERMON IV.
On Lent II.

Published by Father Abbot Giovanni Crisostomo Trombelli among the Opuscula of the Ancient Latin Fathers, vol. II, part I, p. 281. He judges it to be Leo's, as indeed we have seen it ascribed to him in our manuscripts of collections 1 and 2, and also in the Venetian Lectionary 153 and Vatican 6452. But in Lectionaries 105 and 107 of the basilica of St Peter, which put his name over the genuine Sermons of Leo, it is placed without Leo's name after his sermons on Lent, together with another sermon beginning *Jejunii tempora*, which we noted in the preface, no. 11, was taken from Isidore of Seville. It is likewise anonymous in Vatican Lectionary 1268. A similarity of doctrine, which will also be

found in Augustine and other Fathers, proves nothing; and the same holds for a similar interpretation of a church text. The style, certainly, more compressed and confined to shorter sentences, differs greatly from Leo's.

CHAP. I. — Dearly beloved to us, your faith does not require [us] to set forth the teachings of religion. For we urge fasting, which for those who live rightly is an increase of devotion, a wall of faith, the overthrow of wickedness. We also counsel that one must abstain not only from foods but always from all vices. Do not be prodigal in revelling, or arrogant in drunkenness: for it is written in Solomon: The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15); and the Apostle too says: Make no provision for the flesh in your desires (Rom. 13:14). Abstain therefore in these days from worldly cares and carnal desires. Let the body be chastised, that the soul may be healed. For hope is strengthened when the flesh is thinned by frugality, and a diet of delicacies nourishes the present life, not the future one: for luxury accompanies abundance of goods. Put away from you the rivalry of envy, despising evil speech and all the seeds of sins. Loosen the snares of violent dealings; and let the deceitful devices of false accusations cease. Provide lodging for the needy and for those of the household of faith. Tear up unjust bonds of debt, so that you may keep fasts pleasing to God not only in body but also in spirit.

CHAP. II. — We must also hope for the fruits of our own fasting from the seed of almsgiving. For it is written: As water quenches fire, so almsgiving quenches sin (Ecclus. 3:33). We must also act so that we are overcome not by zeal for avarice but by concern for mercy. We ought to abstain from lavish display. Let us give temporal things to the poor, so that by their prayers everlasting gifts may be granted to us. For by the exchange of a little bread and money, freedom from punishment for sins is conferred on us. It must also be known that the Lord made many poor, just as he made many rich: so that there may be need to entreat the Lord, and that you who have suffered none of these things may fear lest perhaps you suffer them. Feed, therefore, you who are healthy, the weak man, as an example of calamity in the flesh. Feed, then, the poor man, you rich man, whose portion perhaps you received from the Lord our God so that you might feed him. Feed the fasting man, lest his share, taken from you, be given to another who is generous. Feed the man dying of hunger: for whoever could save a man by feeding him and has not fed him has killed him. Let the desires of silent beggars also be anticipated; for we read: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the evil day (Ps. 40:2). Let us therefore give alms to the needy before they ask, lest, hesitating from excessive need, they seem to be exacting it from us by crying out. Let us provide them with at least some portion of the heavenly gifts bestowed on us, lest through sloth we pay penal interest to our creditor (Luke 16:2). Let us think of that rich man who, because of the crumbs of bread [supply: denied to the poor man], asked for a drop of water and did not receive it. Let us recall that widow who, by putting two coins into the treasury (Luke 21:2), offered to the Lord all the living she had. Let us too give to our brothers at least what is surplus to us. Nor indeed ought we to carry out the divine commands sadly, like hypocrites; but let us give thanks to God, the author of our generosity, and, praying constantly, let us provide the needy with the means of temporal life, that we may attain eternal life; through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON V.
On the Passion of the Lord I.
From the manuscript Lectionary of St Alexander in Columna at Bergamo, where it is attributed to St Leo; but the author is later,
who at the beginning of the sermon excerpted some things from Leo's Sermon 52, On the Passion 1, ch. 4.

CHAP. I. — After that first and universal ruin of human transgression, by which through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death (Rom. 5:12), no one would any longer escape the dominion of the devil, no one the chains of dire captivity; nor would reconciliation to pardon or return to life lie open to anyone, unless the Son of God the Father, coeternal and coequal in all things, deigned also to be the son of man, and for the whole redemption and salvation of humanity was hung in the flesh on the cross. For this was the cause of the redemption and salvation of the whole human race: that God himself in man truly suffered, and truly died, and truly rose from the dead, so that he might truly open the gates of the heavenly kingdom to men who believe in him and die in his will, and redeem us from eternal night and punishment. For he endured many and various injuries for us, not because his own faults demanded it, for he never committed any sin, but solely because of our need, who had been bound with such hard chains, and cast down into so deep an abyss of death, that we could not be set free except through his immense clemency, through his human passion and death, unless he by his death took eternal [death] away from us, unless he broke the powers of the devil and led [us] with him to the heavenly kingdoms, and granted to all of us who wish to remain in his will a sweet and easy road to the heavenly kingdoms.

CHAP. II. — Therefore, dearest brothers, what must we do in return for such great benefits of God, except die to the world and its lusts? Mortifying carnal desires in ourselves by vigils, by fasts, by chastity, by endurance of adversity, by perseverance in goodness, by prayers, let us continually commend ourselves to God, repenting, lamenting and confessing our sins, and redeeming ourselves from eternal punishments by alms, so that, thus upheld by divine aid, we may deserve to remain in eternal blessedness there whither the Lord our God has led us back by his death: through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON VI.
On the Passion of the Lord II.

Inscribed to Leo in the same Bergamo Lectionary. It seems to be by the same author as the preceding sermon; for some things are likewise excerpted from Leo's Sermon 50, On the Lord's Passion 5, ch. 1.

CHAP. I. — The true ground and chief cause of Christian hope, dearly beloved, is the cross of Christ: which, though it is a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1:23), because it seemed unworthy to them that the Son of God should suffer such injuries for the salvation of the world, is nevertheless to us the power of God, by which we believe we have been set free, and the wisdom of God, by which we believe and understand, indeed know, [that we are] from God, abiding in the work of his commandments. Hence this highest and most powerful mystery of divine mercy must always be held in our hearts with all reverence, but above all when the return of the Lord's passion is celebrated. And to us nothing that was done for us, humbly and sublimely, in the Son of God seemed either impossible according to man or unworthy according to himself. Let us truly believe and venerate all this, and not condemn it as a stumbling-block with the impious Jews, nor as foolishness with the unbelieving Gentiles. For the just and merciful God, who made us and redeemed us when we were dead through sin, willed to exercise the power of his Godhead for our redemption. But he willed also that this be done by human passion together with the power of his dignity, so that lost man might be set free through man.

CHAP. II. — Thus, then, medicine was bestowed on the sick, reconciliation on the guilty, thus redemption on captives, so that the just sentence of human condemnation might be undone by a just work of liberation. For if the Godhead alone set itself against [the devil] on behalf of sinners, it would conquer the devil not so much by reason as by power. So the Son of God admitted impious hands to kill him in the body, that he might destroy eternal death in the whole human race, and gloriously lead the human race itself to eternal immortality and blessedness and the fellowship of the angels. And in all the things that the madness of the Jews insultingly and insolently inflicted on him, our sins were washed away, our offences were expiated: because human nature, which had been guilty through sin and captive, suffered in Christ innocent and free from all fault, that he might take away sins and grant to all who believe in him pardon of offences through repentance and confession.

CHAP. III. — Therefore, brothers, let us remember continually at how glorious a price we have been redeemed, and from how harsh a condemnation by the devil we have been set free. Let us strive, as far as we can, with the Lord's bounty, to imitate so glorious a redemption of ours by good works; and whatever we have done too sluggishly and slowly in these days toward our correction or amendment, let us at least in these few days work out our salvation most zealously. Let our fasts be fruitful, so that what is withdrawn from our own body may restore the flesh of a needy neighbour. Let the one who offends against us receive forgiveness, so that we may deserve from God forgiveness of sins. Let our confession be pure, our penance severe, our prayer tearful, our vigils constant, with works of mercy. Let the desire of the flesh be put to death, so that the eternal salvation and glory of our soul may grow. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for all ages of ages. Amen.
SERMON VII.
On Palm Sunday.

Now first edited from four Lectionaries, Vatican 1276, St Peter's Basilica 106, the Padua [Lectionary] of the Eremitani 112, and another of the chapter of Verona; in these, although it is attributed to Leo, its style nevertheless does not savour of Leo.

CHAP. I. — You have heard, dearest brothers, the Scripture of the Hebrew exodus and the words of the mystery: how the lamb was sacrificed, and how the people were saved, and how Pharaoh was struck through the mystery. Understand, dearly beloved, how the paschal mystery is new and old, temporal and eternal, corruptible and incorruptible, mortal and immortal. Old according to the law, but new according to the word; temporal through the type, eternal through grace; corruptible through the sacrifice of a beast, incorruptible because of the Lord's life; mortal because of the burial, immortal because of the resurrection. The law is old, but the word is new; the type is temporal, but grace is everlasting; the sheep is corruptible, the Lord incorruptible: broken as a lamb, but raised up as God. For he was led like a sheep to the sacrifice, yet he was not a sheep; and [he was] like a lamb without voice, yet he was not a lamb: for those things were done in figure, these are found more truly. In place of the lamb there is God, and in place of the beast he was made man. And the man is Christ, in whom all things are contained. For Isaiah says: Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, without voice, so he did not open his mouth. In lowliness his judgement was taken away: who will tell of his generation? (Isa. 53:7–8)

CHAP. II. — Many other things indeed, and more besides, were foretold by the prophets concerning the paschal mystery of Jesus Christ. For he was led as a lamb, slain as a sheep; he redeemed us from the worship of the world as from Egypt, and saved us from the hand of the devil as from the hand of Pharaoh; and he sealed our souls with his own spirit, and the members of our body with his precious blood. This is he who brought death to confusion and set the devil in lamentation. This is he who struck down iniquity and injustice, as Moses condemned Egypt to barrenness. This is he who rescued us from slavery to freedom, from darkness to light, from death to life, from tyranny into an everlasting kingdom. This is he who endured many things in many. This is he who in Abel was slain, and in Isaac was bound by the feet, and in Jacob was a wanderer, and in Joseph was sold, and in Moses was wrapped up, and was exposed in the river by his mother, and in the lamb was slaughtered, and in David was persecuted, and in the prophets was dishonoured. This is he who was buried in the earth, and rising from the dead ascended to the heights of the heavens. This is the lamb without voice, this is he who was taken from the flock and sacrificed as a victim at evening, who was buried at night. This is Jesus Christ our Lord, who rose from the dead and raised man from the lower tomb to life.

CHAP. III. — This one, then, was killed in the midst of Jerusalem. By whom? By Israel. For what cause? Because he cured their lame, and cleansed their lepers, gave light to the blind, and raised the dead. What have you done, O Israel, so new an injustice? You dishonoured him who had made you noble. You disgraced him who had glorified you. You rejected him who had proclaimed you. You killed him who had given you life. Is it not written, You shall not shed innocent blood (Deut. 19:10), lest you die most wretchedly? 'I,' says Israel, 'did this, because he had to suffer.' You are mistaken, O Israel, when you think like this. He had to suffer, but not through you; he had to be hung on the gibbet of the cross, but it ought by no means to have been done by your right hand. With this cry, Israel, you ought to have called to the Lord: 'O Lord, if your will has so decreed that your Son should suffer, yet let him by no means suffer through me. Let him rather be judged by foreigners, by the uncircumcised, let him be fastened with nails by any tyrant you like. Far be it that these impious things be done through me.' With this cry, O Israel, you were quite unwilling to call out, nor did you refrain from laying your own hands on your Lord. You are not among his works. Did it strike no shame into you when a withered hand was restored sound to its own body? nor when blocked eyes had been opened? nor when loosened limbs were made firm by his voice? Nor did you blush at that recent miracle, in which one already four days dead rose from the tomb at the command of his voice? O Israel, you saw such great wonders of Christ, and did you remain always in unbelief? You indeed, passing over all these things, prepared the Lord for death. For you prepared the sharpest nails, false witnesses, gall too, and a sword, as for a murderous robber. You also brought blows upon his poor body, and set a crown of thorns on his head, and those good hands of his, which had formed you from the earth, you bound with cords, and that good mouth of his, through which you were fed with life, you fed in return with gall. On the great day of the feast you killed your Lord. And you enjoyed rich food, while he suffered the hunger of famine. You drank wine and ate bread; but he vinegar and gall. You were splendid in body, and he was worn down by sorrows. You exulted, and he was afflicted. You sang psalms, and he was judged. You led dances, and he was laid in a tomb. You lay on a soft couch, but he in a sepulchre and coffin. O most impious Israel, who committed this new injustice, subjecting your Lord to new sufferings, you killed your Ruler and your Maker, who honoured you, who gave you the name Israel. But you were by no means found to be Israel.

CHAP. IV. — You did not see the Lord, nor were you willing to understand God. Did you not know, O Israel, that this is the Firstborn of God, who was begotten before the morning star (Ps. 109:3)? This was he who led you into Egypt, and there, preserving you, provided you food. This is he who was sent to you, who healed your parents, who raised the dead. This is he against whom you acted wickedly, whom you slaughtered. This is he whom you sold. Therefore, O Israel, because you did not tremble over the Lord, you trembled when attacked by enemies; you did not fear over the Lord, you did not wail over the Lord, [but] you wailed over your dead sons. Because you forsook the Lord, you will not be found by him either. You dashed the Lord down, and you too will be dashed to the ground. And you lie on the ground; but he, rising from the dead, was carried up to the height of heaven. Now therefore come, all you families of men who are mixed up in offences, and receive remission of sins. For I am your remission, I the Pasch of salvation, I the Lamb who was slaughtered for you, I your redemption, I life, I am your salvation, I am your resurrection, I am your King. I will raise [you] up by my right hand. This is our Lord, who made heaven and earth, who was hung on the tree, who was buried in the earth, who rose from the dead, ascended to the heights of the heavens; who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.
ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING SERMON.

In the Latin editions of St John Chrysostom it was published under Chrysostom's name as Homily 7 On the Resurrection, and is still read there. It is also read, inscribed with Chrysostom's name, in the Breviary of the monks of the Cassinese Congregation. But since it is plainly the work not of a Greek but of an ancient Latin author, like the other sermons of those same editions wrongly attributed to Chrysostom, it is accordingly absent from the Greek editions of this doctor. Further, in the manuscripts of collections 1 and 5, and in two more recent Lectionaries, Vatican 6451 and 6452, we found it inscribed to Leo; and Fr Giovanni Crisostomo Trombelli, who did not consult the Latin editions of Chrysostom, printed it as if unedited under Leo's name, from a Bologna manuscript of collection 2, among the Opuscula of the ancient Fathers, vol. II, part I, p. 231, where, however, he judged it falsely ascribed to Leo. The style does not differ much from Leo's; and the recurring formula 'dearly beloved', repeated four times, might seem to point to our Leo. The author is certainly Latin, and indeed a bishop of some Western Church in which the rite flourished of reading the chapter of the Gospel of St John, In the beginning was the Word, on the very day of Easter, or in the vigils of Easter, as these words indicate: 'The Evangelist who was read says, And the light which shines in the darkness, etc.', and also those put near the end: 'You have heard the evangelist saying today that whoever believe in God, these are sons of God. For he gave power to become sons of God to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.' These words, spoken to the neophytes baptized in the night, well suggest the reason for reading that chapter: namely, that from that reading they might understand the divine gift by which the Son of God, born a son of man, raised men themselves, reborn through baptism, to the dignity of sons of God. But since no documents of the Roman Church edited by Cassander, Hittorp, Mabillon, Fronteau, Cardinal Tommasi and Martène show this rite, although they are later than Leo's age, they nevertheless prevent anyone from affirming Leo to be the author of this sermon. This rite, however, was well known in Africa, as we learn from Augustine's Sermons 119 and 120, in which the same chapter of the Gospel is expounded; and the Maurist Fathers, in note 1 on Sermon 119, think these sermons were preached not on Easter day but on the night of Holy Saturday. Hence this sermon seems to be assigned to some African. And so that no doubt may remain, two Vatican Lectionaries, 1270 and the very ancient 3835, inscribe it to Augustine; and that it suits him equally is confirmed by an ancient interpretation of verses of Psalms 117 and 125, which we find expressed in the same words in Augustine. This one sermon, although formerly published among Chrysostom's works, we have inserted in the appendix because, being the most worthy of Leo of all, it could be corrected in several places from our codices.
SERMON VIII.
On the Resurrection of the Lord I.

CHAP. I. — Although all the solemnities, dearly beloved, which are celebrated in the churches for the honour of God are holy and venerable, yet today's day of the Lord's resurrection has a festivity of its own. This is so precisely because all other days contain in themselves only the joy of the living, but this one also the gladness of the dead. This festivity, then, is common to those below and those above together: for the Lord, rising from the dead, gave festivity both there where he conquered death and here, where he returned as victor from death. And therefore the Psalmist rightly says of this day in particular: This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it (Ps. 117:24). For in announcing the Lord's resurrection he proclaimed a day of saving exultation not only for those above but also for those below, because when the Lord descended into the dark gloom of the underworld, without doubt even then there was a most splendid day there, where the Saviour shone forth. Hence the evangelist who has been read says beautifully: And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it (John 1:5); for although the Lord descended into the darkness, he did not feel the obscurity of the darkness. The light of the everlasting nature kept, in that horror of night, the inviolable splendour of its majesty; as if the light was not overcome by the night, but the night by the light.

CHAP. II. — Let us therefore be glad, dearly beloved, and exult in the Lord. For today the light of salvation has been given us by the Lord, according to what the same Psalmist says in what follows: The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us (Ps. 117:27). And what is added further: Appoint a solemn day with crowded gatherings, up to the horn of the altar; this too I see fulfilled today in the Church of God. For since she is full of devout assemblies up to the horn of the altar, the fullness of holy Church has fulfilled the Scripture itself. This day, then, dearly beloved, is the day of resurrection and life. A more delightful rejoicing of faith makes it more welcome after Lent: for to the sorrow of the guilty days of remission have been joined, so that reward may follow patience at once, according to the saying: Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy (Ps. 125:5). Whoever, then, of you sowed in tears, take the rewards of exultation. Let each one know that the greater the seeds of weeping he sowed, the greater the fruits of joy he reaps. So the image of the beatitudes to come is already contained in things present. For just as now there is relaxation after strictness, so in the future there will be rest after labour.

CHAP. III. — Hence I beseech you, dearly beloved, together with the whole Church, especially you who, reborn into new salvation, have put on white garments, that you keep the gift you have received pure and spotless, that you preserve the brightness of your dress in your way of life as well, and that your hearts be as white as your garments. You heard the evangelist saying today that whoever believe in God, these are sons of God. For he gave power to become sons of God to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:12). So you too are now not brought forth from a conception of the flesh, but begotten of God the Father. It remains that you preserve, through a holy life and way of living, the dignity of your holy origin. And truly, according to what the Apostle says: As newborn infants, endowed with reason, desire milk without guile, that by it you may grow unto salvation (1 Pet. 2:2). And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.
SERMON IX.
On the Resurrection of the Lord II.
Now published from the Lectionary of St Anthony at Padua, where it wrongly bears the name of Pope Leo.

CHAP. I. — On this holy day, dearest brothers, on this renowned and excellent day, on this day of which the most sacred psalm sounds out: This is the day which the Lord has made (Ps. 117:24): on this day sorrow was taken from the hearts of the disciples, and confusion was put before the eyes of the Jews. On this day of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ the disciples, filled with sorrow, were going each wherever he could: there was no one to gather them, because what is written had already been fulfilled: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered (Zech. 13:7). The tomb, however, was sealed with the seal of the Jews and secured by a guard of soldiers: inside was the light, which could not be bound at all. For whatever we seal we can bind entirely; light we cannot bind. And therefore the eternal light, who in the beginning illuminated the world, and who both was and is and will be always with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one in Trinity and Trinity in unity, he himself, God and man, through his wonderful resurrection deigned to touch the hearts of the faithful with the key of his truth, so as to illuminate what was dark and open what was shut. He who, with an angel ministering, was joined to the Word, he himself, with an angel ministering, was today raised again from the tomb. As if a seal could in any way hinder him in whom there was no deceit, guards are posted to guard a man. Him whom they already knew to work miracles, cast out demons, cleanse lepers, raise the dead — could he not bring himself forth from the tomb?

CHAP. II. — But by now the crowd of the Jews, blind in heart, who had the law and did not understand it, were singing the third psalm, yet did not recognise the Trinity of the Lord. For the third psalm has: I slept, and took my sleep, and rose again, because the Lord upheld me (Ps. 3:6): while, that is, intent on and ready for the confusion of the disciples, they deserved to find the confusion of their own souls. For they say to Pilate that that deceiver said he would rise on the third day; let soldiers be posted, they say, lest his disciples come and steal him (Matt. 27:63). If the tomb was closed to the disciples, could it be closed to the holy angels? Or perhaps he could not rise from a sealed tomb, who could come forth from a sealed Virgin?
