The Virgin was truly sealed, and the burial was truly sealed. The true Virgin gave birth without a man, and the true seal on the tomb became a door. For while those guards are present, no longer guards but witnesses, they could guard, but God had determined to raise his Son: for the angel of the Lord had come down from heaven; seeing him, the guards are terrified. They could not see that exalted angel, being full of the falsehood of the Jews. The women are allowed to see the angel, because they had come weeping to the tomb. To them he spoke great joy: I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified: he is not here, but he has risen, as he said: come and see the place where the Lord was laid (Matt. 28:5). O joy not only for those women, but for all the faithful and believing who are reborn! He has risen, he says.

CHAP. III. — But to say briefly what had been foretold long ago: that King David, full of the Holy Spirit, truly sang in the psalm: The Lord rose up as one sleeping (Ps. 77:65). Why should I say a great deal at length? Let what speech cannot unfold suffice for faith. Who can grasp the heavy labour of the night just past, who the splendour of this day? This day has poured out boundless joys for all Christians, since Christ has made it better for us than the other days. Let us exult, then, dearest ones, and be glad in it, for this is the day which the Lord has made. For I think, brothers, that this day alone is to be called great, the day on which the true Day was raised again for us. For this day shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. By darkness I mean the Jews, who, in denying Christ the Day, lost the light they had received: for while they cry, Crucify, crucify, darkness came at midday. So, because the Jews wished to seize Christ by night, they therefore remained in darkness. But the Gentiles and the dwelling nations, who departed from the darkness of idols, deserved to be made day, as the Apostle says: Who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his majesty (Col. 1:13); whence he also says in another place: We are, he says, sons of light and sons of the day (1 Thess. 5:5); we are not of the night or of darkness: let us walk honestly as in the day (Rom. 13:13). Let us exult, then, dearest ones, all with all, for this is the day which the Lord has made.

CHAP. IV. What has your iniquity profited you, serpent, I say, or what has your persecution availed by its cruelty? Behold, he has risen from the tomb whom you Jews fixed on the wood. Today he was seen alive who was thought slain. Fortify carefully, Jew, the tomb of your cruelty, add guards of soldiers, order watches of the secret night hours, so that you may prove dead him whom you refused to acknowledge alive. You gave Judas the disciple a price in silver, so that you might put Christ, once slain, in the tomb: give as much silver to the guards, so that you may hear the falsehood that he was stolen by the disciples. Pay out, pay out silver for your crime. You keep watch at the tomb by night only in vain. Already he has risen, already he has ascended the heavens, already he has been glorified for our sake, who humbled himself for our sake. For what are you going to do, made from friends into the fiercest enemies? He whom you fixed on the wood with such zeal sits himself at the right hand of the Father in heaven; he is the one who comes in the name of the Lord, God the Lord, and he has shone upon us. He has shone upon us, and has put you under our feet. For the Father has fulfilled for us what he promised to his Son. For what has he fulfilled for us, and what did he promise to the Son? The psalm says. The Lord, it says, said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet (Ps. 109:1). For behold, Christ sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven, and he has put you Jews under our feet on earth. When, fierce Judaea, you bought him whom you were to kill, you should have kept for yourself what you had bought, and not lost what you had. Behold, you have lost the silver, and him whom you bought you did not possess.
SERMON X.
On the Resurrection of the Lord III.
From the same Paduan codex of St Anthony, in which it is attributed simply to Leo.

CHAP. I. The Gospel of Christ is most fully set forth when his resurrection is preached. For the Gospel Scripture holds that many miracles and signs were done by the Lord. Yet he did none greater than when he rose with his body and lifted earth into heaven. In this resurrection of Christ there is both a miracle and an example: a miracle, that we may believe; an example, that we may hope. For what he himself did in the beginning, he has promised to us at the end. The impious, who are called unbelievers and pagans, and the carnal Jews believe that Christ was slain. It is no great thing, then, to believe that Christ died: for this the unbelievers too have in common with us. They themselves believe that Christ died. But we believe the death because of the resurrection: for if death had not gone before, there would have been no resurrection. Whoever denies that Christ died also denies the resurrection. Whoever professes that Christ died must still be dealt with, so that he may also believe that he rose again: and so it will be well with us with the Lord God.

CHAP. II. Now let us endure the present, let us love the things to come: let us not be delighted by the blandishments of the world, let us not be broken by the terrors of the world. When God coaxes us, he promises eternal life; and when he frightens us, he threatens with Gehenna. However much the world coaxes, [God] has that delight of which the psalm says: Delights 424 in your right hand even to the end (Ps. 15:11). There Christ, already seated, protects with his right hand. Thence he shows himself to be our head. He sees his members toiling, he sees his body harassed in great temptations; and do you think that the head takes no care for its body? If your eyes can fail to take care that you do not stumble; or your ears refuse to hear the remedies by which you may be healed; or your tongue be unwilling to speak about your wound; or your hands can refuse labour, so as not to help some toiling member of yours; then our Lord Jesus Christ too can fail to care what we do, or how we toil. What need is there for us to say it? Hear him himself crying out: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? (Acts 9:4). The one to whom he spoke thus on behalf of his members, he wished to make his member. May the Lord Jesus Christ deign to make useful members of us too, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON XI.
On the Ascension of the Lord.
Edited by Quesnel from a codex of St Peter of Corbie, in
which it is attributed to St Leo.

CHAP. I. Today, brothers, the victory of Christ is completed; today his triumphal banners are raised. Hell grieves with its prince over its despoiling; the heavenly host rejoices over the restoration of its loss. Today that flesh which was lifted up from the earth has been set at the right hand of the Father, because all natures have been laid low before it, and every principality and power has bowed down before it. Today the new way, of which the Apostle speaks (Heb. 10:20), has been inaugurated for us: because through the flesh of Christ the entrance to heaven, through which no flesh had passed before, has been unbarred; which [way] the same Apostle calls living, because it has been prepared for the members of Christ who are to enter by it in their time. Today the opening of the book is accomplished, which no one could open except the Lamb who was slain: since its mysteries have been revealed, when the things found in the law and the prophets were fulfilled today, the dispensation of his humanity being completed. Christ first descended, to become a sharer in our nature; at the last he ascended, to make us sharers in his glory. Descending, by his life in time with visible miracles he as it were suckled infants; ascending, he gave gifts to men, so that, instructed [Al. nourished] and as it were brought up to manly strength, they would no longer seek his temporal sight, but would strive with all their desire to follow where he had gone before them.

CHAP. II. Since, then, we have been bereaved of his temporal presence, let us hasten with all our intent towards the eternal sight of him. Let us say to him in the words of the Psalmist: My heart has said to you: I have sought your face; your face, Lord, 425 I will seek: do not turn your face from me (Ps. 26:8). For the whole dispensation of Christ's humanity aimed at nothing else, did nothing else, than to direct our intent to things above, and, when the time of our mortality is fulfilled, to lead us to the open sight of himself, and to satisfy those so led with the eternal glory of his face. For, as the Apostle testifies, We shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Hence the Psalmist: I shall be satisfied when your glory is made manifest (Ps. 16:15). These are the good things of Jerusalem, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered the heart of man: which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9). These good things the Psalmist beheld, as far as he could, in a riddle, when he said: For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I wished from you upon earth? (Ps. 72:25). He said in wonder: What is there for me in heaven, etc.? because he was not able either to unfold the greatness of the heavenly glory in speaking or to comprehend it in thinking.

CHAP. III. Let us therefore hunger for these things, thirst for these things, since for this the supreme High Priest ascended as forerunner for us into the true Holy of Holies, that is, to the right hand of the Father, to confirm the hope of his members that the lowliness of the flock will follow where it believes its shepherd has gone before. For so the Lord himself promises his disciples: Where the body is, there the eagles too will gather (Luke 17:37). He calls eagles the saints who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1:23). For the nature of eagles is said to be that they perceive carcasses beyond the sea by their sense of smell, and hasten there in swift flight to satisfy their hunger. This hunger of eagles, then, signifies the desire of holy souls, which, thirsting [An. perceiving] with the nostrils of faith for their head, set in the highest rest beyond the whirlwinds of the world, would wish by the flight of hope to stand in the presence of the Creator, and to rejoice without end in the fullness of his face. This indeed is the meaning of this solemnity: that meanwhile we follow him as on the twin wings of the virtues, namely charity and hope; so that when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father (1 Cor. 15:24), we may reign with him without end.

CHAP. IV. Therefore, as the Psalmist urges, since the Lord has reigned, let the earth exult (Ps. 96:1), that is, the Church; let it exult in faith, since you, Lord most high over all the earth, are exalted exceedingly above all gods (ibid., 9). Let it exult in hope, since we shall be filled with the good things of your house. Let us cry out from the marrow of our hearts with the Apostle: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress? Or famine, or nakedness, or the sword? (Rom. 8:35). For when he has led us from hope to sight, God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). He himself [will be] food and drink, he himself clothing, and all things that can honourably be thought of and desired by all. Let the soldiers of Christ covet this donative, and not desert their service, until, the contest completed, they receive from their emperor the unfading inheritance.
426 SERMON XII.
On the Most Holy Trinity.
Now published for the first time from the Lectionary of the chapter of Verona, in which it is headed: Homily of St Leo, pope, on chapter XV of the Gospel of St John, verse 26.

From many places of the holy Gospel we find that the disciples, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, were less able to understand the secrets of the divine sublimity, and less strong to bear the adversities of human wickedness. But when the Holy Spirit came upon them, together with an increase in the knowledge of God, they were given the steadfastness to overcome the adversities of this world. Hence it is now said to them by the Lord's promise: When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me, and you will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning (John 15:26). It must be noted first of all that the Lord testifies both that the Spirit of truth is to be sent by himself, and immediately adds that the same [Spirit] proceeds from the Father; not that the same Spirit proceeds from the Father in a different way than he is sent by the Son, but the Son [says] that he is both sent by himself and proceeds from the Father so as to indicate that the Person of the Father is one and his own another, and to declare that within this same distinction of persons his operation and will are one with the will and operation of the Father. For when the grace of the same Spirit is given to men, the Spirit is indeed sent by the Father [and] sent by the Son; he proceeds from the Father, and proceeds also from the Son, because his sending is itself his procession, by his own free will, since, just as he is coequal with the Father and the Son, so he has the same will as the Father and the Son. For the Spirit breathes where he wills (John 3:8); and as the Apostle says, having listed the heavenly gifts: All these things one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11). And the Holy Spirit, on coming, bore witness concerning the Lord: because, breathing into the hearts of the disciples, he revealed to them in clear light all that mortals were to understand about him, namely that he became equal and consubstantial with us at the end of the ages, that, born of a Virgin, he lived in the world without sin.
The end seems to be missing.
427 SERMON XIII.
On the Feast of St Vincent the Martyr.

We found it ascribed to Leo in the Vallicelliana manuscript XV, whence in some editions it was placed after Leo's Sermons. It was first relegated to the appendix by Quesnel, and is presented here as revised by him with two manuscripts; he also, in the admonition inserted in our preface, not improbably conjectured that the author was a Spaniard. This judgement of Quesnel is approved by the Maurist Fathers, who, since in most codices this sermon is attributed to Augustine, reprinted it in the appendix to Augustine, vol. V, sermon 188.

CHAP. I. Although, dearly beloved, one faith makes the glorious passions of all the martyrs, whom places distinct by region have been privileged to have, worthy of veneration by all with undivided honour, yet in this homage of veneration those claim for themselves a dignity of their own who have both built up the Church of God by their teachings above the rest and helped it by their patronage. Among these we rightly celebrate with catholic zeal the blessed deacon Vincent, through whose confession and death we unhesitatingly acknowledge that Christ was preached to unbelievers. He, in order to commend the devotion of the faithful more zealously to God, blazing with a loftier affection of charity, at length faithfully offered himself to death, so that the strength of faith founded on that most solid rock, Christ, might be given to his followers for imitation; and also that the seed of apostolic preaching, scattered by him among many, kept safe by the help of his intercession and replenished with the fruit of perfect completion, might be stored in the Lord's barns in heaven. Let his own [land], then, venerate him the more, whom even foreign [lands] admire: so that he may show himself more generous in benefits to those to whom he knows himself more lovable in rejoicing, and that on his feast there may be a richer compass of joy, from whom the effect of faith has grown.

CHAP. II. His spirit, then, shone with so great a gift of virtues that, supported by the office of sacred ministry, he who was to follow the Son of God, our Lord, in his passion first ministered the cup of the same Christ to believers for salvation. Happily inebriated in mind by drinking it, he approached undaunted the madness of the rabid enemy raging against Christ, endured it with restraint, mocked it securely, knowing that he was prepared 428 to resist, and not knowing pride as the means by which he would conquer: because, fortified with spiritual arms, he resisted out of love for him by whose help, invincible, he conquered by bravely suffering whatever punishments the rage of the one raging against him devised. Therefore neither the plates of the fiery gridiron, nor the rack, nor the hooks and iron hands, nor the fearsome strength of those beating him, nor the pain of torn limbs, nor the crackle of the fire and the salt crackling as it was cast into his opened entrails, could in any way subject him to the command of Dacian. But while the swelling of his frenzy grew so great that he would exultantly boast that he had either conquered or killed the man subdued by such pains of suffering, he was cheated of the hope he had conceived, and, from that by which he seemed to appear the victor, by that he was compelled to blush as the vanquished: since the harder the punishment with which the martyr of God was pressed, the greater the steadfastness of confession in which he exulted. Hence, brothers, it is good to look over or recall more clearly the very last parts of his passion: so that your holiness may observe to what end the devil led his minister by his wiles, and how Christ preserved his servant to the very end.

CHAP. III. In which this was indeed wonderful: that as much as the one was crushed and constrained outwardly by manifold kinds of punishment, so much was he enlarged inwardly as the inner man exulted; and as much as the other was puffed up outwardly with the boasting of temporal power, so much inwardly, perceiving himself despised, was he tormented in the inner man and choked. Seeing himself despised, he raged, and could find no one on whom to inflict further vengeance. For he saw that the hands of the raging executioners found more wound in him than body, and that the spirit alone, still vigorous, reproached his folly the more, the more the rule of truth provoked it. Wherefore, believing that he would remove the cause of his confusion if he removed the person who had spurned him, and that Dacian would blush less if the people did not see Vincent, he ordered him to be removed from public view. But so that not even thus should he be free of punishment, broken potsherds were strewn beneath him where he lay: so that the force of their sharp points might tear the more the cut-up mass of the body laid upon them, and the limbs, given back to torment, might meet the fragments that would cut them.

CHAP. IV. Yet blind cruelty is deceived in its belief that it is conquering. For the divine goodness, accompanying its beloved more fully in his confession, brings new light into the darkness, and renders the dark prison 429 a splendid tabernacle. The healing hand of God cherished the torn limbs, and made good the damage of the dug-out side with a more beautiful increase of his former health. Struck, therefore, by the unwonted brightness of this light, the guards were astonished; and the mind of the pale gatekeeper also trembled at the voice of the angels singing a hymn to God together. The servant runs, half dead, to the governor, whom the report of the message would strike more heavily than the blow of a sword: and since he could not, from the greatness of the matter, keep silent about what he had seen, trembling seizes the judge, grief tears him, fury inflames him; and so that Vincent, conquering in his punishments, should not obtain the glory of martyrdom, "Quickly," says Dacian, "let him be brought out of the prison, lest, while we persist in punishing the rebel, we seem rather to crown him with victory." He is brought out, therefore, from that abyss of the foul prison, more beautiful indeed by heavenly grace, and, if he were still to suffer, stronger. But when he understands that the desire of one striving toward the call of the kingdom could not be broken by any kind of punishment or death, [he orders him] also to be comforted with gentler rest: that is, so that if, with the executioner removed for a little, he breathed out his soul in quiet, it might be said that he was not killed but died: as though punishment had not slain him with whom punishment itself also perished.

CHAP. V. Meanwhile the heavenly court receives blessed Vincent, and grants him the gift of blessed happiness. At his entrance the angelic spirits rejoice, and all the saints, his fellow citizens, congratulate him together. And we give thanks to you, Lord Jesus, that [this is] a soul worthy of your fellowship, which stubbornly bore torment and fled lying submission; and which, content that the persecutor raged, disdained that he should spare [it]. Learning, then, of his holy departure, the insane judge Dacian, not knowing that Christ had conquered in Vincent, promises himself vengeance by exposing the corpse of the one whose victory through his virtue he bewails. For, with the pride of his fury deceived, he orders the lictors to throw [him] out to be consumed by wild beasts and dogs: so that by such food he might fill the belly of those whose mind he himself bore. But so that, as the divine benefits increased, the grace of a greater victory might be conferred on Vincent, a raven is sent, a bird fond of corpses, to guard, while fasting, the exposed banquet of the body.

CHAP. VI. Here, dearest brothers, here observe the distinct services rendered to merits. Elijah once, cautiously avoiding the impious hands of Ahab and Jezebel (3 Kings 17), is fed in the desert with ravens serving him; but Vincent, the champion of truth, slain by the rage of Dacian, is exposed to be consumed by wild beasts; yet, with a raven serving him, he is kept unharmed. Elijah, then, obtained by the divine will, with ravens providing, the means to be fed: to Vincent it was granted, a raven likewise serving, that he should not be eaten. And the raven, to show that it had been appointed his guardian from heaven, drove off from a distance, with no sluggish onset, the other birds as they approached: among them also a monstrous wolf coming nearer, as one who presumed with sacrilegious boldness to defile the treasure entrusted [to the raven], it drove far away, beating it with feathers and wings. But the wolf, stupefied, showed by a certain bearing of its own that it had come not so much to inflict injury as to increase the splendour of the miracle. O shameless fury and foolish madness! The raven serves, the wolf reveres, Dacian persecutes, and in his ferocity he does not blush still to wish to destroy one whom the ferocity of beasts, made tame, was busy protecting.

CHAP. VII. Therefore, to hide the martyr's praise, he chose now not a secret place but the deep: believing that not bolts but the seas would serve him to conceal his glory: as though the same one were not lord of the element, through whom the hidden recesses of the prison had lately shone for him, radiant with heavenly brightness. The body is given to sailors to be sunk in the waves, so that at least the seas might help him, for whom the earth had failed to conquer the soldier of Christ. And so, when they had sailed out over the depths of the strait for a great distance, the almighty right hand of God followed the body cast among the engulfing waves, and that which had borne the spirit into heaven soon brought back the body to the tomb. Thus the preacher of truth, dearest ones, is neither conquered by the pains of torments, nor overcome by the confinement of the dark prison. He is not torn apart by beasts, he is not hidden by the deep, but is given back to the shore and made famous by proclamation, so that he who had truly confessed the name of the Godhead might experience in truth the support of the divine goodness present to him. His life, glorious in virtue, the grace of a precious death so adorned that what he taught by living he steadfastly confirmed by dying; and it was fitting that he should attain through death to the vision of him to whom he had always borne witness by the conduct of an approved life: knowing that from contempt of the present life rises the glory of eternal blessedness: by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING SERMON.

Quesnel edited the following sermon, inscribed to Leo, from a Paris codex, mutilated, that is, lacking its end. We present it complete from the manuscripts Vat. 1271 and 6454, that is, with some chapters added which cohere with the preceding ones both in style and in content, and complete the sermon.

The same Quesnel prefixed to this sermon a notice in which he seemed to claim it for St Leo: "The following sermon," he says, "on the Chair of St Peter, which we publish, was supplied to us by an old manuscript codex of the Royal Library, marked number 341, from which we copied it. It has Leo's name prefixed in the codex in this way: On the Chair of St Peter the apostle, sermon of St Leo the pope; nor is there doubt that it is our [Leo's], so far as can be detected from the style, which seems to me altogether to accord with Leo's, nor does anything occur for which it ought to be denied to our pontiff. This certainly is beyond doubt: that this sermon was delivered at Rome and by some Roman pontiff, as can be argued from many places, and that many phrases and words familiar to Leo are found here. Peter, says this [author], was set over (praelatus) the people of God; this word, rare in that sense, is read in letter 12 (now 14), ch. 11: Let him, then, who knows that he is set over certain people not take it ill that someone is set over him. Here he praises the fiery companies of the heavenly spirits: Leo writes of Paul as fiery, of the heart being set on fire, of the Holy Spirit setting on fire, in places noted in dissertation 2. The bounty of divine grace, the left-hand number of the goats, cautious provision, incautious severity, the snares of raging beasts, from the mouth of truth, and many other modes of speech represent Leo, who speaks similarly in his certain writings. What is found in this sermon about church singing and about the adornment of churches will, I think, suggest to no one any sign of a more recent age: for St Leo often mentions singing, while the adornment of churches used on feast days is proved not foreign to Leo's age by Leo's sermon 40 (now 41) alone, which is the third on Lent, right from its beginning. The antiquity of the feast of the Chair is established, both from a very ancient list in Gilles Boucher, in which it is thus given: 8th day before the Kalends of February, the Feast of Peter's Chair; and also, and more certainly, from canon 22 of the second Council of Tours. For if at that time, that is, in the year of Christ 566, it was kept in Gaul, it must doubtless long before have been celebrated in the Roman Church. Indeed the same canon proves that it was already ancient even then in the Gallican [Church]. For the superstitions, for whose cutting off it was enacted, probably began to creep in only after long spaces of time from the institution of that feast. Add that in the first times of the Church this custom flourished, that the day of consecration of those bishops who were more celebrated was celebrated every year, as is clear from the example of Sts Gregory the Great, Ambrose, Basil and others. With how much better right, indeed, ought the pontificate of the prince of the apostles and primate of the Church to be recalled with an annual feast, at least in the Roman Church, where he had fixed his see. Moreover, since a twofold commemoration of the Chair of St Peter has now been established by the decree of Paul IV, Roman pontiff, of the year 1557, one on the 18th day before the Kalends of February for the Roman, the other on the 8th day before the Kalends of March for the Antiochene, it is agreed that formerly there was a single solemnity in the Church, on the 8th day before the Kalends of March, on which the memory of both, or rather in general the assumption of St Peter to the episcopate, was celebrated with due honour. And it continued in the Roman Church up to the decree of Paul IV, which was received in use very late by the Gallican Churches, as is clear from the Breviaries and missals; but even today it is not received by some. For the rest, since the sermon on the Chair of St Peter which circulates under the name of St Augustine has long since been relegated by learned men to the appendices as a spurious offspring, there is no monument of that feast that approaches the antiquity of this one. From which also the list of Sylvius, already partly edited by John Bolland, is shown to be either supposititious, or at least corrupt in that place where, instead of the feast of the Chair on the 8th day before the Kalends of March, it has the deposition of both apostles noted. More on this feast can be seen in the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, both in the Annals, vol. I, and in the Notes on the Martyrology, and also in our most learned Charles Le Cointe, author of the Ecclesiastical Annals of France, vol. II, at the year of Christ 566, no. 18 and following." Although he had established this in its place in the first edition, after weighing the matter more maturely, in the general preface which he printed last, he regretted having attributed the sermon to Leo. But in the preface of the second edition, no. 3, he says: Having examined the matter again and weighed the style, we return to our first opinion, not daring to deny this sermon to Leo. It is indeed most surprising that it could have seemed to a man versed in reading Leo that the style of the following sermon accords with Leo's. For, first, the formula in ch. 1, Dearly beloved brothers, and that repeated twice in ch. 3, Dearest brothers, are altogether foreign to Leo's sermons. Next, the barbarous adjective discordabile in ch. 2, and (to say nothing of the whole syntax, manifestly dissimilar) the words in ch. 3 in which he calls St Peter, counselling us, the consul of the heavenly court, are too repugnant to Leo's Latinity and manner; so that the words fiery, giver of grace, and others of that kind contribute nothing, since they will be found similarly not so much in Leo as in other writers, as we read in the Life of St Honoratus written by Hilary, no. 3, God the giver of grace, [no.] 32, to his fiery speech, etc. Of the same kind are the chapters we have added. For, to omit the allegorical expressions senators of the world, in the heavenly court, starry kingdoms, those words especially in ch. 5, that we may return with the steps of our tongue to you, my brothers, who live in Christ, are most foreign to the style of our Leo. Moreover, what is related in the same chapter about the multitude of simoniacs living in luxury suits a later age. Hence, since several manuscripts agree in bearing the name of Leo alone, this is perhaps the offspring of some Leo, Roman pontiff, who flourished in a later and more corrupt age. Further, what Quesnel remarks about the deposition of the apostles Peter and Paul noted on the 7th day before the Kalends of March in the Calendar of Sylvius is to be compared with what we shall establish about his Calendar in the observations on sermon 82, no. 4.
433 SERMON XIV [Otherwise, among the Leonine sermons, XCVI].
On the Chair of St Peter.
Edited by Quesnel from a manuscript codex of the Royal Library, and supplemented from the Vatican [manuscripts].

CH. I. Dearly beloved brothers, the glorious solemnity of the blessed prince of the apostles is here, which we ought to take up with all eagerness of soul and celebrate with all devotion of mind. For since the day of his martyrdom is rightly held most illustrious throughout the whole world, this [day] is to be celebrated with no less joy by the whole holy Church. For on that [day], while the hymn-singing choirs of angels sang in turn, he was crowned beyond all words; but on this [day], while throngs of the faithful rejoiced on every side, he was raised with great glory to the pontifical chair. On that [day] he ascended the throne of heaven for his own blessedness; but on this he obtained the primacy of the holy Church for our salvation. On that [day] he was joined to the fiery companies of the blessed spirits, 434 so that he himself might receive eternal rewards; but on this he was set over the people of God, so that he might call us all to eternal rewards. That festival, then, belongs chiefly to the angels; but this one belongs especially to the faithful peoples. But through the grace of him who slew the enmities in himself, making peace in one new man (Eph. 2:16), what could have been proper to each has been made common to all, that is, to men and to angels.

CH. II. Let us therefore keep this solemnity of ours, so to speak, dearly beloved, with a twofold joy, as is fitting, and celebrate it not only outwardly but also inwardly with the full desire of the soul. On this side, then, let the harmonies of those who sing sweetly resound; on that, let the concordant movements of souls answer in turn. Let the church be adorned with lights; let the conscience shine with virtues. Let the floor of the basilica be cleansed of filth; let the temple of the inner man be purged of vices, as Paul says: The temple of God is holy, which you are, and 435 the Spirit of God dwells in you (1 Cor. 3:17). Let nothing out of tune be detected in our voices, nothing discordant be found in our conduct. For the holy day has its own dignity, and our mind has its own solemnity: the former, namely, that there be rest from the toilsome business of this world; the latter, that there be abstinence from the heat of earthly desire and from the allurements of all vices. The former, that it may shine with visible ornaments; the latter, that it may gleam with virtues. But since we have received so excellent a shepherd on this day from the bounty of divine grace, with what rashness do we attempt to open our mouth to speak to you on our own part? Let us therefore behold with the eyes of faith our most blessed pontiff, raised on the episcopal seat, crowned with priestly fillets, speaking to his people in his own person, and preaching in the assembly of the holy Church in his accustomed manner. Let him himself say in his own person what he decrees must be done both by you and by us. Behold, O our most blessed shepherd, we your sheep are present together, and we humbly beseech you to give us the nourishment of your teaching. But we cannot even be sheep unless you yourself instruct us how we ought to put on the fleece of innocence. For you say: As newborn infants, desire the rational milk without guile, that by it you may grow unto salvation (1 Pet. 2:2).

CH. III. Now since we have heard how we ought to become sheep, it remains for him to show us how we may also escape the left-hand company of the wanton goats. I beseech you, he says, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which war against the soul (1 Pet. 2:11); and so that he may confirm by outstanding example this mortification of the flesh which he teaches by word, he says: Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps (ibid., 21). Now keepers of cattle are accustomed carefully to restrain their flock from harmful plants, and to move to distant pastures in search of wholesome grazing; and while they forbid some [plants], guarding against death, they offer others, restoring life. For in one place they withdraw what is harmful, in another they allow what will be beneficial, lest, while [the flock] fasts from poisonous fodder by careful foresight, it should also be kept from wholesome [fodder] and waste away through incautious strictness. Since, then, our shepherd restrains us by forbidding the deadly pastures of carnal desires, he now loosens our mouths toward the wholesome green fields of our hope. For he says: Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, by which he has called us into a living hope, into an inheritance undefiled and unfading, kept in the heavens (1 Pet. 1:3). Let us therefore, dearest brothers, attend with the ears of our hearts raised to the voice of our keeper, the blessed apostle Peter, and, holding the straight line of his 436 footsteps, let us never stray from the pastures to which he calls. For if we willingly accept his counsel, we shall not fear the ambushes of raging beasts. For does not our keeper watch carefully over his flock, and cry out with anxious voice that the attacks of wild beasts must be guarded against? For the devil, he says, as a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour: resist him, strong in faith (1 Pet. 5:8). It is fitting, therefore, dearest brothers, that we listen with attentive hearts to the consul of the heavenly court as he counsels us, and that we fear to make light of the most certain counsel for our salvation. For this is he who heard from the mouth of Truth: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven. This is he who heard: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven (Matt. 16:18, 19).

CH. IV. He ought not, therefore, to be despised by man in his preaching, who deserved to be honoured by the Creator and Redeemer of men with the privilege of so great a dignity. It is a terrible thing for the counsel of him to be carelessly disregarded to whose power both heaven and earth are subject. He who shuts and opens heaven binds and looses earthly things at his own judgement. For indeed the chair of ecclesiastical primacy was divinely handed over to him, so that it might be founded with perpetual firmness. For from the beginning of the world we know there were many chairs among the people of God, not only good but also bad (but in the chair of Peter Christ both utterly overthrew the bad and confirmed the good with eternal stability). For of the good it is said: Let them exalt him in the church of the people, and praise the Lord in the chair of the elders (Ps. 106:32), [namely those] who keep in their works the precepts of the teachers of the holy Church. Moses held the chair for the people of Israel, of which Truth itself said: The scribes and Pharisees have sat on the chair of Moses (Matt. 23:1). But on the other hand, of the chair of the reprobate it is said through the Psalmist: Blessed is the man who has not walked [in the counsel of the ungodly], and has not sat in the chair of pestilence (Ps. 1:1). For he sits in the chair of pestilence who teaches the people the plagues of error.

CH. V. Chairs of this kind the Lord mystically overthrew when he cast out of the temple both those who sold and those who bought. For it is written: He poured out [the money] of the money-changers, and overturned the chairs of those who sold doves (John 2:15). This chair of pestilence that Simon the magician sought to acquire when he desired to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit. But the hand of the apostolic tongue overthrew it before it was built, 437 and cut off the pestilent heresy at its very root as it was being born, saying: For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of sin. You have no part nor lot in this matter (Acts 8:21-23). By this sword of the apostolic sentence all are run through who either gape to buy ecclesiastical honours or do not fear to sell them. Their wretched multitude is seen even today in the holy Church, who do not fear to possess the gift of God against the Lord for their own lust; who indeed, though outwardly they seem alive, already stink, buried in the perpetual death of damnation. They count it as nothing to seek the gain of souls, and they nourish their most wretched flesh in delights and in the stench of luxury. Against them I think it better to be silent than to say a little. For a few words do not suffice to tear apart and rebuke their deadly peril, against whom heaven and earth and all the elements bring testimony of damnation. Now, therefore, we cease to speak against dry bones, so that we may return with the steps of our tongue to you, my brothers, who live in Christ.

CH. VI. Let us therefore, dearly beloved, found the dwelling of our mind on the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, so that it may remain unharmed by every assault of adversity, after the example, that is, of the prudent man of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: He who built his house upon a rock: the floods came, the winds blew, and beat upon that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon a rock (Matt. 7:24, 25). Let us recall to mind what is said through Paul: We cannot rejoice here with the world and reign there with the Lord; and again: Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:21). Behold, this blessed apostle Peter, whose festival we keep today, who was so dear and intimate to our Lord Jesus Christ, who received, by his gift, such great power not only on earth but also in heaven, nevertheless entered the starry kingdoms through the martyrdom of the cross.

CH. VII. Therefore, dearly beloved, constantly putting to death our flesh with its vices and desires, let us keep the apostolic precepts most zealously, because we are to render account of our deeds with these very men as judges. For to them it was said: Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19:28). They are the senators of the world, of whom it is written: Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land (Prov. 31:23). Founded, then, on their faith and instructed by their teachings, let us strive with divine help so to lead this mortal life in time that we may deserve to rejoice with them without end in the heavenly court, with our Lord Jesus Christ proclaiming [perhaps: granting it], to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON XV.
On the Annunciation of the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary.

This sermon is wrongly ascribed to Pope Leo in two Lectionaries of St Benedict of Polirone, and in one manuscript it is placed after another sermon for the same feast, likewise attributed to Leo, which we mentioned in the preface to this appendix, no. 30. Just as we proved there that that sermon is an ancient version of a sermon of St Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, so we believe, not improbably, from the similar thought and manner of writing, that this one too is an unpublished translation of another sermon by the same author, especially since it is known that several of his orations are missing.

CH. I. The coming of our Lord and Saviour, by which, clothed in the human race, he deigned to visit us, the universal Church keeps throughout this whole age, and by its yearly return it becomes very joyful. For what the world, believing it was done once for the redemption of its own salvation, received, it has consecrated to posterity to be celebrated for everlasting generations; and it brought it about then that from the old life joy should be born in newness of mind. Now, therefore, the miracle of time past is set before our eyes, while the divine readings solemnly present the things that were done long ago, and they are celebrated most devoutly year by year. Behold, we heard, when the holy Gospel was read, that the archangel Gabriel was sent by the Lord from the royal thrones, promising a son to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:26). For entering in to her, who in modesty lay hidden from men in a secret place, he greeted her with this opening of speech: Hail, Mary, he said, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you. O wondrous announcement! O strange greeting, bearing an abundance of fullness and illuminating the virginal breast! The angel therefore came down, gleaming in flame-bearing flight, lighting up both Mary's dwelling and her mind with the brightness of his splendour. A herald going before the judge, so glorious and gentle, so swift and hastening, so that in the praetorium of virginity, which remained secret on earth, the Lord of majesty might be received, he said: Hail, Mary; hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you (ibid. 28). He who created you has already chosen you beforehand; he whom you are to bear has already filled you.

CH. II. So she was troubled at his entrance, and was considering who had blessed her so; and she, keeping within herself the modest silence of her holy resolve, and unacquainted with a man's address, is troubled as the angel greets her, and is astonished at the one blessing her in such a way; yet she did not dare to speak before the speaker. For wondering within herself for a long while, she pondered in her mind with fear why she was so blessed. And while she hesitated, pondering at length, and [trying] to observe more closely the angel's presence (for, weighing at once the radiance of his presence together with the blessing, she hesitated in silence), Gabriel, the illustrious archangel, envoy of the most holy Trinity and sharer in heavenly secrets, looked upon her and said: Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; he will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:30-33). Then Mary, listening to these angelic words with weighed examination, and weighing them on the balance of her mind, the most prudent virgin said: How shall this be which you say, since I do not know a man (34)? Shall I have a son, I who know no man? Shall I carry an offspring, I who [have] no mother's milk? With dry breasts, from where shall I give suck to the lips of an infant asking to suck, when neither inborn youthful love has possessed the bed of my chamber, nor has a husband's embrace ever been granted it? And the angel said: Not so, Mary, not so. Do not be afraid; do not be anxious about the integrity of your holiness. You will remain untouched, and you will rejoice in offspring, in a son. Without union with a mortal man you will become the daughter-in-law of the Most High, because you are to bear the Son of God. And Joseph, that chaste man adorned with the name of just, not your husband but your guardian, will not come near you; but the Holy Spirit will come upon you; you will not burn with carnal desire, nor will a bridegroom cleave to you, but the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one that will be born of you will be called the Son of God (ibid. 35). O dwelling worthy of God! Until the angel, by most clear testimony, had proved to her what had been brought from the hall of the Father's palace, and of what kind it was, so that she might receive it with her own ears, she uttered no word with her modest mouth, no assent in reply. But when Mary heard that her unharmed virginity was confirmed by truthful assurance, she answered at once, fitly arranging in her most holy breast the secret chamber that was to be: Behold, she said, the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word (ibid. 38). As if she were saying: My heart is ready, because my womb remains untouched. Let it happen to me, archangel Gabriel, according to your word. Let him come to his dwelling who has set his tabernacle in the sun. Let the Sun of Justice rise for me who remain a virgin, in whose wings everlasting healing abides; who, flowering in perpetual chastity, decreed that integrity should endure in her. Let him go forth as just brightness, and let the Saviour be kindled like a torch. The sun's torch lights up everything, and penetrates within the particular things that perhaps seem to obstruct its rays, and destroys nothing at all. Let him now come forth before the eyes of men, beautiful in form above the sons of men; let the bridegroom come forth from his bridal chamber, for I have been made secure about my resolve.

CH. III. Who, my brothers, will be able to tell this generation in speech? Who could unfold it with tongue or eloquence? The inviolate virginity of nature is preserved, and the infant grows within the virgin. And when the time was fulfilled that she should give birth, the sacred offspring was brought forth, the manner of whose conception no human father knew. This is the ineffable nuptial union of the Word and flesh, of God and man. For thus between God and man was made the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5); and therefore the virgin's womb was chosen as the most precious bridal chamber of the marriage, so that, since the world had become squalid through filthy sins, the Creator of the world, coming without worldly act, poured forth into the world from pure entrails, and born in the world by a new miracle, might render the world clean. For the Son of Man came, as the Son of God and man himself says, not to judge the world but to save the world (John 3:17). Tell me now, I beg you, holy mother of the Holy of Holies, who without the furrow of human propagation and without the rain of carnal seed brought forth in the bosom of the Church the fragrance of the morning flower and the snowy lily of the valleys: tell me, I beg, unique mother, with what hands or by what joint of the Godhead he formed in your womb the son whose father is God alone. Tell, I beseech you by God, who made you such that he himself might be made in you: tell me, I say, what good you did; what price you offered; through what powers you canvassed; what patrons too you had; what votes you promised; by what sense or what thought you arrived at receiving these things, that the power and wisdom of the Father, which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1), remaining wholly everywhere, and coming into your womb without any change in himself, should so inhabit the chaste fortress of your womb that entering he did not harm it, and going out he kept it unharmed? Tell me then, how did you arrive at this? And she: You ask me what gift I offered to become the mother of my Saviour? My offering is virginity; my promise, not given by me to myself, but granted to me by the author of all good himself. For every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (Jas. 1:17). My canvassing is my lowliness; and therefore my soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour, because he regarded not a tunic studded with gold, not displays gleaming with hidden gold for the adornment of my neck, nor did he look at stones of precious pearls hanging in my ears, nor heed a blush of the cheeks coloured with deceitful paint; but he regarded the lowliness of his handmaid (Luke 1:46-48). For the meek one came to the lowly one, as had been promised beforehand by the prophet's prophecy, which says: Do not fear, daughter of Zion: behold, your King comes to you, meek and gentle, sitting upon a cloud (Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:5): that is, upon the Virgin Mary, whom he provided for himself as mother, a star without equal.

CHAPTER IV. So the meek one came, resting upon a maternal spirit that was lowly and quiet and trembling at his words. So the meek one came, filling the heavens, passing through the lowly to the proud, and he did not leave the heavens. Those puffed up with the swelling of pride he himself healed like a gentle physician, applying the plaster of lowliness. O deep lowliness! O more excellent height of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and his ways past tracing out (Rom. 11:33)! The bread of angels is suckled at his mother's breasts. The fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 4:14) asks the Samaritan woman, who prefigures the Church, for a drink (ibid. 7). He does not refuse to feast with sinners, he whom the households of the heavenly dignities serve with trembling. The King of kings restored the official's son to health (ibid. 50), not applying a poultice of various ointments, but carrying the medicine on his tongue. He cures the centurion's servant, worn out by fevers, whose faith was found praiseworthy (Matt. 8:10; Luke 7), because the centurion believed that it would be done by the Lord's power just as he himself gave commands to the soldiers under him. So too [he took on] the sufferings of the paralytic (Matt. 9:2; Luke 5:20), as the Lord, by mercifully visiting her, healed the woman's long-standing affliction (Matt. 9:22), in which the humour of the disease, like bilge-water, had made her limbs wasted. The Saviour himself, sensing her silent faith, dried up the fountain of troublesome blood flowing out of her bondage. And how shall I run through everything? Time fails in telling with what magnificent power and deep goodness he accomplished all things, he who, great towards the small, lowly towards the proud, came down full of mercy. He did new things for the world, who came new into the world. Of his wondrous form the evangelists display their figures: man, lion, calf, eagle. Man from a virgin mother without a man; like a strong lion he lay down in death; and by his own power he was lifted up on the cross, like a young calf willingly slain in his passion for the sins of the people; and like a mighty eagle, rising from the tomb with his body taken up again, cutting the air in close flight, he trampled the falls of all, and ascended above the Cherubim and flew; he who walks upon the wings of the winds ascended into heaven: to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON XVI.
On the Feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

Although this sermon belongs to the appendix of collection 2, whose sermons we showed to be spurious in the preface prefixed to the Sermons, no. 19, and for that reason they were also omitted in the Casanatense manuscript of the same collection, yet since it is cited as Leo's from a manuscript, apparently of the basilica of St Peter, on the testimony of Peter Mallius, which we quoted in the same preface under the same number, we thought it should be placed in the appendix, lest anyone perhaps suspect that a genuine sermon had not been found by us. The author seems to be some Roman pontiff.

CHAPTER I. Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the feast of the two holy apostles Peter and Paul, whose sound and preaching have gone out into the whole world. Thus their passion is celebrated from the East to the West, since they suffered for the King of heaven and earth. The city of the Romans deserved [this], where the memorials of the apostles are set. For the preachers of the kingdom of heaven had to be there where the kingdom of the Romans was established, so that various nations coming there might honour the memorial of fishermen. For those who know it, on the way to the blessed apostle Peter stands the memorial of the emperor Hadrian, a temple built of wondrous size and beauty; can anyone say, 'Let us go into the emperor's memorial'? So the emperor's memorial is passed by, and people hasten to the fisherman's memorial. They who were born fishermen became good fishermen. Fishers of fish became fishers of men, as the Lord Christ said: Come after me: I will make you become fishers of men (Matt. 4:19). I do not change your craft for you: I change the kind of fish. You used to draw the living out of the sea to death; now you will draw the dead out of the world to salvation.

CHAPTER II. One was a fisherman and the other a persecutor. How much did persecutors and fishermen deserve, that they should become preachers? First in the order of the apostles Peter was chosen; last in the order of the apostles is Paul, as he himself testifies of himself, saying: For I am the least of all the apostles (Rom. 15:9). He who chose the first also chose the last, so that first and last might suffer together. A good passion, which now is joined to praise. A good contest, which martyrdom completed. The apostles knew towards what crown they were reaching, which Peter and Paul received in the city of Rome. For the Lord said in the Gospel: Whoever leaves father or mother, wife or children, and all that he possesses (Matt. 19:29), or whoever loses his life for my sake in this world, will keep it for eternal life (Matt. 10:39).

CHAPTER III. So, brothers, we must not love life for the sake of life: for the sake of eternal life the temporal must be despised. Good disciples, who held the true teaching of their master, finished the course, kept the faith, loved the promises, despised temporal things, and possessed eternal life. One was grafted in from a countryman; the other was made a lamb from a wolf. Of the apostle Paul it was said: A ravening wolf, in the morning he will seize, and in the evening he will divide the food (Gen. 49:27). Saul was a persecutor; but he was changed, so that he became Paul the preacher: he was formerly a persecutor, but afterwards he became a magnificent preacher. Christ, whom he once blasphemed, he afterwards preached publicly; for he himself testifies of himself, saying: I who was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor; but I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief, so that God might reveal his Son in me (1 Tim. 1:13; Gal. 1:16). This he granted to me, the persecutor. But what did he grant to the fisherman, if not the keys of the kingdom of heaven? For Peter's faith merited the keys of the kingdom of heaven, because he was first to acknowledge the Son of God. O glorious merit of the apostles! They were not chosen for glory on one day, but on one day they won the palm. They were not chosen for the apostolate on one day, but on one day they merited to receive consecrated martyrdom. They passed beyond the heavens, and ran to the Lord God.
SERMON XVII.
On the Feast of the Blessed Apostle Paul.

From a codex of collection 2 it was recently edited by Abbot Trombelli. Besides the manuscripts of collection 2, we found it in the Monte Cassino codex of collection 1, and also in two Vallicelliana Lectionaries, VII and A 6, everywhere bearing the name of Pope Leo. But in two Vatican manuscripts, 1272 and 3835, this heading is read without any definite author's name: Likewise by the same, on the Feast of the Blessed Apostle Paul; which usually signifies that this and the preceding sermon have the same author; and in both codices it is preceded by a sermon ascribed to St John Chrysostom. But since the author of this sermon is certainly Roman, there is plainly exposed here the carelessness of some copyist, of the kind we mentioned in the preface, no. 9: namely, that he copied this sermon with the same heading from an older Lectionary, although he did not excerpt the preceding sermon, to which the true author's name was prefixed in the same book. The Roman author is later than Gregory the Great: for in his time, as the Micrologus testifies (On Ecclesiastical Observances, ch. 42), the feast of St Paul began to be celebrated on the day after the feast of Sts Peter and Paul. Indeed, in sacramentaries older than the Gregorian, namely the so-called Leonine and the Gelasian, the feast of both apostles is assigned to the same day, and no separate Mass proper to St Paul is set out for the following day, as is first found in the Gregorian. This sermon, mutilated in most manuscript copies, we were able to find complete only in the very ancient Vatican 3835.

CHAPTER I. Twofold, dearest brothers, are the joys of today's festival renewed, as we keep the yearly feast of the teacher of the world. Therefore, exulting in the Lord and rendering immense praises to his ineffable majesty, let us rejoice with great gladness. And surely we ought to be glad with most abundant delight: for whenever the memory of the saints is celebrated, the minds of the faithful are filled with very great joy, and are greatly illumined with spiritual progress, because their presence is not doubted. So as we gather, dearest ones, in this most holy hall, we believe that the same distinguished preacher stands in our midst, and in a certain spiritual and invisible way rejoices together with us on this his most celebrated solemnity. And therefore, dearly beloved, no bodily sloth should entangle any Christian from hastening to this venerable church, where his holy body rests. But above all it is fitting that all who live in the city of Rome and the neighbouring regions should hasten as quickly as possible before everyone else. For if all people from the farthest parts of the world, fearing neither the hardship of a very harsh journey nor the long distances of land, long devoutly to present themselves at the threshold of the apostles at whatever time they can, what excuse can the Roman citizens offer for neglecting, though present on the spot, at least to come to their festival, when they are known to be protected by the prayers, defence and aid of these same apostles?

CHAPTER II. For yesterday, the day on which the princes of the apostles themselves were crowned with martyrdom, we hastened with most devoted affection to the church of the blessed apostle Peter and celebrated his solemnity. For it was fitting that the festival of him who was found worthy to obtain the primacy of the apostolate should be celebrated first. Today, however, we keep the feast of the teacher of the Gentiles and the illuminator of the whole world. For although both received the prize of martyrdom together, yet because of the crowds of people flocking together there was reason to transfer the solemnity of the blessed apostle Paul to another day, so that, just as the whole multitude gathered in the hall of blessed Peter, so the same congregation of the people might likewise flock together into the church of his fellow apostle, which is joined to it, and all might have an equal devotion in rejoicing. But see, many, given over either to sloth or to worldly cares, have put off coming to this hall of the most excellent blessed apostle Paul. Therefore, dearest brothers, every care of worldly thought must be cast aside, and the desires of temporal gain rejected, and all of us, running together with whatever effort we can to celebrate the memory of the saints, and above all the feast of the blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, should come together, devoutly assembled alike in the churches of both, so that, just as divine favour made them illustrious as equals with the insignia of honours, so human devotion may hold them alike in their solemnities.

CHAPTER III. For this most blessed man, first indeed Saul and afterwards Paul, first, I say, a persecutor, afterwards a preacher, infected with the savagery of Jewish belief, burned with an excessive madness of ferocity against the Christians. For, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9:2), having received power from the chief priests to bring bound to Jerusalem any of the Christian religion he could find, he was going, raging, seized by great fury, and suddenly, illumined and terrified by the brightness of a heavenly ray, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad (ibid. 4). And at once, falling to the ground, he lost the light of his eyes. O the great kindness of the mercy of our almighty God! O the inestimable mercy of [his] long-suffering! He terrified him a little, so as to console him many times over. For he struck Paul, so as to heal him beyond measure. For at once the Lord commanded Ananias to grant him the grace of regeneration in baptism and to bestow on him the light of his eyes that he had lost. For a sheep was commanded to lead a wolf to the fold and to make him a sheep like itself. For Ananias is interpreted as "sheep". The sheep feared to come near the wolf; [yet] it approached, and seeing him turned to gentleness by divine correction, at once conferred on him the gift of baptism, applied the standard of Christ, and placed him in the Lord's fold. O the power of a wonderful working! The sheep made the wolf a sheep, because it received the strength of the good shepherd; and him whom it first had as its most savage assailant, it afterwards received as its gentlest fellow combatant. The Lord, having him predestined before all ages, declares him a vessel of election, and announces that he will carry his name among the Gentiles.

CHAPTER IV. O blessed Paul, distinguished preacher, how glorious and praiseworthy you shine among the apostles and all the martyrs! For although you are seen to have come last into the fellowship of the apostles, you are shown to have laboured more than all in the Gospel of Christ. See, your most luminous teaching shines out in the whole world. With what praises can a human tongue worthily glorify you, most excellent prince of the apostles and most renowned preacher of the truth, whom the Redeemer, mercifully calling from heaven, made a worthy worshipper of himself, a most choice vessel and a most vigorous athlete? Hence, lawfully fighting the good fight and finishing the course of your ministry (2 Tim. 4:7), caught up for this even to the third heaven, you were found worthy to hear secret words; for the rest, receiving the crown of justice laid up for you, and the worthy reward of your labours from the just judge, our Lord, you rightly triumph for ever with the angels in the heavenly kingdoms. Wherefore, as we venerate this your most sacred solemnity, glorious prince of the apostles and teacher of the Gentiles, do not cease to commend us with constant intercessions before our Creator, for the true confession of whose name you obtained the palm of martyrdom; so that, surrounded by the special support of your intercessions and fortified by your continual protection, we may be found worthy to be rescued from all the adversities of this flowing world, and, celebrating with sincerity of mind and in security the joys of your most devout festival, may be able to reach the eternal kingdoms, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for all ages of ages. Amen.
