SERMON XVIII.
On Saint Peter. How he was led out of prison.
Now first published from a Monte Cassino manuscript.

CHAPTER I. How Saint Peter was bound in prison with two chains and handed over to four squads of four soldiers, and also how he was freed from there by an angel of the Lord (Acts 12), your love has heard in order. Saint Peter, then, was sent into prison for the sake of the name of Christ, but he could not dread the punishment of prison, because in prison he himself was a temple of God. He was bound with two chains, but in that very prison he was drawing the chains of crimes off believers. He was guarded by four squads of four soldiers, but under that very guard he was making the four Gospels known to those coming to faith. And it is no wonder indeed if he could not fear a human guard, who was kept by a divine guard. So while Peter was carefully guarded in prison by four squads of four soldiers, bound with two chains, an angel of the Lord came to him, as your love has heard, and opened the doors of the prison, and said to him: Rise, and take your garment and cover yourself, and put on your shoes, and come, follow me (ibid. 8). And he rose and followed him, and when he had come with the angel to the iron gate, at once the same gate opened to them of itself. And it is no wonder indeed if the gate [opened] to Saint Peter, who had already received the gates of the underworld into his power, as the Lord said to him: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of the underworld shall not prevail against it. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven (Matt. 16:18). So he who threw open the gates of the underworld opened the iron gate for Saint Peter. He who destroyed death itself rescued Peter from death.

CHAPTER II. But what was then done for Saint Peter according to the letter, we recognise is also done mystically in our case, if we follow the faith of Peter. For we too are placed in this world as in a prison. If, then, we are found worthy to be visited by the Lord, an angel of God is sent to us, and says to each one of us: Gird yourself and put on your shoes, and cover yourself with your garment, and follow me. We gird ourselves if we encircle the loins of our body with the band of chastity, as the Apostle says: Let your loins be girded (Luke 12:35) in chastity. We also shoe our feet if we fortify the steps of our life with the precepts of the Gospel faith, so that we may safely trample the thorns of sin and the thistles of iniquity. We also cover ourselves with a garment if we keep in ourselves that wedding garment, that is, the grace of baptism. Let us then faithfully fulfil these things: at once the chains will fall from our hands, that is, the chains of sins, by which we were held bound and tied in the soul. But we cannot escape from the prison, that is, from the error of this world, in any other way unless we are visited by the Lord through an angel. The iron gate too is opened to us, that is, the gate of death, and the punishment which the Son of God shattered by the power of his passion; and then we shall come to the house of Mary, that is, to the Church of Christ, where Mary the mother of the Lord dwells, and there a girl named Rhoda will meet us. And such a name, Rhoda, fits the mystery of our salvation. For Rhode in the Greek language means "rose". So as we come to the house of Mary, a girl named Rhoda meets [us], that is, the congregation of the saints, which shines like a rose with the glorious blood of martyrdom.
ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING SERMON.

In accordance with our practice, by which we promised that all of his would be inserted in this edition, we are obliged to present Quesnel's lengthy note. "Whether this sermon," he says, "was delivered on the feast of the seven Maccabean brother martyrs, or on the feast of the seven brothers, sons of the martyr St Felicity, that is, Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis and Martial, who were crowned with martyrdom in the time of the emperor Antoninus, there will perhaps be some who doubt, if they turn their eyes for a moment from the title, whose reliability, like that of others of this kind, it is not wrong among the learned to call into question. And although the memory of the latter was celebrated at Rome from ancient times, since they had ennobled that very City by their contest, yet we judge that this sermon was devoted to the triumph of the former, that is, the Maccabees: both because it mentions the history of their martyrdom as having been read from the sacred Scriptures: 'The cause of today's solemnity, dearly beloved,' he says, 'you have learned most fully from the reading of the sacred history'; and because it attributes such a martyrdom not to the belief of a Roman emperor or prefect, but to the impiety of a most savage king.

"Further, St Leo indicates that another feast was joined to this solemnity of the martyrs, namely the anniversary, as he says, or dedication of a church, by whose consecration he asserts further on that the ancient festival was doubled. But whose church's anniversary, and whose consecration this solemnity was, he himself does not reveal, nor has anyone after him taken the trouble to inquire: because, I suppose, all have held it for certain that this is to be understood of the dedication of the basilica of St Peter in Chains, since even today the festival of that dedication and of the martyrdom of the Maccabees is one and the same, fixed on the Kalends of August.

"But we can by no means accede to this opinion. For the basilica of St Peter in Chains was built by Eudoxia, wife of the Augustus Valentinian, on the Esquiline hill, whence it was also called the title of Eudoxia; and this does not at all agree with what Leo says about this place. For it is plain that the basilica whose consecration was then being commemorated was built not by a woman but by a man: 'A magnificent builder of walls,' he says, etc. Next, all the things that Leo sets out must fit the man who erected the basilica we are inquiring about: namely, 1st, that he had the building raised at his own expense and by his own munificence: 'A magnificent builder of walls,' etc., 'by dwelling in what he founded.' 2nd, that he himself consecrated or dedicated the church: 'Who on this day doubled the ancient festival by the consecration of this place.' 3rd, that the same man had the care of souls: 'But a more magnificent builder of souls'; indeed, that he also discharged the office of teaching in the city of Rome, and therefore that of bishop: 'by doing what he taught.' 4th, that he was one whose memory the Romans could venerate with due honour and join to the solemnity of the martyrs: 'Venerate with due honour,' he says, 'not only the martyrs and the mother of the martyrs, but also the memory of him who on this day doubled the ancient festival by the consecration of this place.' 5th, finally, that he was a contemporary of Leo and had performed works of piety before the eyes of those he was addressing, so that by the memory of them, no less than by the sight of the church they beheld, they could be kindled to progress in virtue; for this is the sense of these words: 'Therefore, dearly beloved, take all the things that you see with your eyes and remember in your mind for the progress of your edification,' etc. None of this can apply to Eudoxia: it must rather apply to one of the Roman pontiffs, to whom alone it belonged to dedicate churches in the City and to act as teachers and builders of souls in it. These things could indeed easily be said of Pope Celestine, who was certainly conspicuous for holiness and is read to have built the basilica of Julius. But I am more inclined to refer them to Sixtus III, the immediate predecessor of our Leo. For first, it is plain that the church whose feast of dedication was then being kept was one of the chief basilicas of the city of Rome, whose dedication anniversary was celebrated by the whole Roman people with such solemnity, such magnificence of festivity, such united zeal and devout spirit, and such a concourse of the people: such beyond doubt was the basilica of St Mary Major, which is also called St Mary of the Snows, and at the Crib, and the basilica of Liberius. That this was rebuilt and consecrated by Pope Sixtus III is attested by the book on the Roman pontiffs, and by Pope Hadrian in his letter to Charlemagne. 'He built the basilica of St Mary, mother of the Lord, which was called of Liberius by the ancients,' says that book under Sixtus III. Of him Hadrian says thus: 'Pope Sixtus, successor of Celestine, built the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, surnamed Major, which is also called at the Crib.' Of this basilica wonderful things are related by Peter of Cluny, Bede, and those authors who have written about the seven churches of the City. Next, it can easily be believed that Leo broke out into the praises of Sixtus on the occasion of the solemnity, since he had been brought up by him, had always attached himself to him as his deacon, had immediately succeeded him as one who had rendered him outstanding service in administering ecclesiastical affairs, and since his memory was also the most recent of all. Finally, he too, as renowned for the praise of holiness, is found inscribed in the ecclesiastical registers among the acknowledged saints on 28 March, so that the holy pontiff rightly said that his memory was to be venerated with due honour.

"There is one thing that could be objected: namely, that the solemnity of the dedication of St Mary is kept on another day, the Nones of August, and that on the other hand no solemnity of dedication is assigned to the Kalends of August in the present Roman Martyrology except that of St Peter in Chains. But what wonder if, over the course of so many years, many things are found to have been changed in ecclesiastical registers of this kind, whose reliability is not in every respect certain and beyond doubt? Moreover, since that most ancient basilica often needed, on account of its age, to be raised anew and consecrated again, just as custom required that the day of its last consecration be held among the feasts, so it was fitting that the memory of its first construction and consecration should not perish, which had become famous throughout the whole world for very many remarkable miracles. For this reason, I suppose, the solemnity of that dedication which had been performed by Sixtus was moved from the first day of August to the fifth, so that the twin solemnity should merge into one and the number of feast days should not grow to the inconvenience of public affairs. And this was especially fitting on account of the other dedication, of St Peter in Chains, whose solemnity falls to be celebrated on the same first day of August."

These things were necessary on the hypothesis by which the sermon on the Maccabees was believed to be Leo's. But they will be recognised as superfluous and useless for the matter in hand if we have shown that this same sermon is not Leo's. For in the very ancient manuscript Lectionary Vatican 3836, which was beyond doubt Roman, for the use of the basilica of Saints Philip and James, where other genuine sermons of Leo are inscribed with his name, this one, on page 1, is attributed not to Leo but to Augustine, with this title: 'Here begins the sermon of St Augustine on the holy Maccabees, Kalends of August.' Who would dare to claim for the Roman pontiff Leo a sermon which the Roman Church herself, by this most ancient testimony, denies to him? It was therefore through the error of later times that it came to be ascribed to Leo in collections 2, 3 and 4, which are of a later age. This one document is most evident to us.

Add that this sermon indicates that the solemnity of the Maccabees was celebrated in the city in which it was delivered. That it was celebrated in Africa is known both from the old Carthaginian calendar, which Mabillon published in the Analecta, and from Augustine's sermons 300 and 301, issued on the same feast, which can also confirm him as the author of this sermon. But that no feast of the Maccabees was celebrated at Rome in Leo's time is gathered from the fact that no Mass of that feast is noted on the Kalends of August, not only in the very ancient Sacramentary attributed to Leo, which will be reprinted in the second volume, but also in the earlier Gregorian Sacramentary, which Ludovico Muratori printed from two manuscripts in volume II of the Ancient Roman Liturgy. And if this feast is asserted in the published Gelasian [Sacramentary], it is certain that this is not a pure Gelasian Sacramentary and that it has received some later additions, among which the Mass of the Maccabees is to be counted, as anyone will understand from the very absence of this Mass in the later Gregorian Sacramentary. This addition could have been brought in from some Church where the feast of the Maccabees was kept, as it was kept in Gaul even in Leo's time; hence their feast is marked in the Calendar of Polemius Silvius, who, as we shall prove in the observations on sermon 83, no. 4, was a Gallic writer and wrote in Gaul.

There is in addition an inscription published by several and most recently reprinted by the abbot Fr Monsacrati in his work on the Chains of St Peter, page 48, in which, among other things, the following is read about the church of St Peter in Chains: 'This temple of the Lord was formerly dedicated to Peter; Sixtus, the third bishop [of that name], had once consecrated it; afterwards it was destroyed in civil war. Eudoxia indeed renewed it entirely there; the blessed Pope Pelagius consecrated it again, laying up there the bodies of the holy Maccabees.' If this inscription were ancient and reported genuine history, so that the celebration of the Maccabees had begun at Rome under Pelagius, before Gregory, still the sermon could not be attributed to Leo. Finally, the formula 'dearest ones', which is inserted at the beginning of chapter 3, is indeed familiar to Augustine but most foreign to Leo's usage; and this indication confirms all the more strongly that the sermon was falsely ascribed to Leo.
SERMON XIX [Formerly among Leo's sermons, sermon LXXXII].
On the Anniversary of the seven holy brothers, the Maccabean martyrs.
Placed now for the first time in the appendix, because it is not Leo's but Augustine's.

CHAPTER I. Thanks be, dearly beloved, to the Lord our God, that your assembly shows how great the solemnity of this day is, even if I am silent. For you have gathered with such united zeal and devout spirit that, even if speech does not declare the magnificence of the festival, the congregation itself bears witness to it. And rightly: for the cause of joy is twofold, in that we both keep the anniversary of the church and rejoice in the passion of the martyrs; and not undeservedly does the Church fittingly exult in the martyrdom of those by whose example she is adorned. The cause of today's solemnity, then, dearly beloved, you have learned most fully from the reading of the sacred history, nor could it escape you what you received as hearers in so great a sequence of deeds, when you honoured with exultant and not silent affection the glorious mother of the seven martyrs, who suffered indeed in each of her sons but was crowned in all. For she followed by a happy end those whom she had sent ahead by her unconquered exhortation. Blessed mother, blessed offspring, memorable the fortitude of those who went before! For when, in that order of deaths and that arrangement of punishments, the impiety of a most savage king had devised that he might promise himself victory both over the first, whom he would torture without the example of endurance, and over the last, whom he would torment by the punishment of others, the palms of the martyrs were multiplied; and while each conquers in all, besides their own crowns they all acquired sevenfold ones.

CHAPTER II. — But these things are to be recalled for a fruitful pleasure of the ears. Knowledge puffs up (1 Cor. 8:1), unless obedience builds up: things heard weigh us down, unless they are taken up to be imitated. For it is not the case that, because the persecutor and torturer have ceased, because all powers now serve as soldiers of God, Christians lack sufferings to overcome. 'Son,' it says, 'coming to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation' (Ecclus. 2:1); and the Apostle says: 'All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution for justice' (2 Tim. 3:12). You, then, who think that persecution has ceased and that you have no conflict with enemies, search the inner secret of your heart, and enter all the recesses of your soul as a diligent explorer; and see whether no adversity attacks you, whether no tyrant wishes to rule in the citadel of your mind. Do not make peace with avarice, and despise the increase of unjust gains. Refuse concord to pride, and fear more to be taken up into glory than to be trodden down in humility. Separate yourself from anger, and let the desire for revenge not inflame the pain of envy. Renounce pleasure, turn away from impurity, drive out luxury, flee iniquity, resist falsehood; and when you see that you have a manifold fight, you too, as an imitator of the martyrs, seek a manifold victory. For as often as sins die in us, so often do we die to sins; and precious in the sight of the Lord is this death too of his saints (Ps. 115:15), when a man is slain to the world, not by the destruction of the senses, but by the end of vices.

CHAPTER III. — If, then, dearest ones, you do not bear the yoke with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6:14), if you cease to be sinners and yield to no temptations of carnal desires, you celebrate this solemn day rightly; and you venerate with just honour not only the martyrs and the martyrs' mother, but also the memory of him who on this day doubled the ancient festival by the consecration of this place: a magnificent builder of walls indeed, but a more magnificent builder of souls, extending his works of piety beyond the limits of his own age, so that devoted posterity might enjoy the benefits of his foundations even in him, both by dwelling in what he built and by doing what he taught.

CHAPTER IV. — All things, then, dearly beloved, which you see with your eyes and remember in your mind, take up for the advancement of your edification, and let each of you so use the dwelling prepared by your forebears as to remember that the temple of God has been founded in himself. Let him place nothing crooked in his structure, nothing weak [...] grow by an indissoluble joining into the unity of the Lord's body: with the help of the cornerstone himself, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.
SERMON XX.
On the Transfiguration of the Lord.
Published now for the first time from the Padua manuscript of St Anthony; wrongly attributed to Leo.

CHAPTER I. — Today, dearest brothers, we solemnly keep the day of him, namely, who, governing all things with the Father, created every day; the Word, I say, which in the beginning said: 'Let there be light, and there was light' (Gen. 1:3). His flesh was glorified today on the mountain, as the Gospel text relates. On the mountain, before two prophets and three disciples, the Lord was transfigured; that is, to give us hope of his Divinity, he willed to show them his face whiter than snow. If anyone wishes to know these prophets, let him run to the most sublime voices of the evangelists. But if Luke seems to anyone to disagree with the two before him, because he states that this brightness of the Lord was shown not after six days but after eight days (Luke 9:28), let him run to the figure of the grammarians. For there is among them a figure called syllepsis, in which many are understood for one and one for many, and the whole is taken for the part and the part for the whole; and let him know that Luke nonetheless described figuratively, including in his Gospel the day when it was promised and the day when it was fulfilled. That is, when the Lord had promised this, it was evening; and when he was transfigured, it was nonetheless already morning. Matthew and Mark, however, passing over the days of the promise and of the transfiguration, preferred to hand down to perpetual remembrance only the six whole days between.

CHAPTER II. — But if anyone should ask why he willed to be transfigured before two prophets and three disciples, let him recall that bright first saying of the Lord himself; he said to the Jews: 'In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true' (John 8:17). And to show that he himself was the one who said to Moses, 'I am who am, and you shall say this to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you' (Exod. 3:14), and who had sent that same Moses to Pharaoh for the deliverance of the children of Israel, and had given him the law on Mount Sinai, and had carried the prophet Elijah in a fiery chariot into the airy heaven, he had brought these witnesses by divine power to behold, with the disciples, the transfiguration of his brightness; recalling, to be sure, one of them from the threshold of death, the other from his translation to paradise. For no one could know the tomb of Moses except him who commanded and brought him to himself; and no one knew where Elijah had been translated except him who had called him to himself. For this is the Only-begotten of the Father, who for the redemption of the human race willed to become the firstborn of his mother. For in this present transfiguration he willed to unite the concord of both Testaments. For to show that he was Lord of the law and of the prophet, he willed to bring these to the testimony of the evangelists. In this transfiguration indeed it pleased him to show to the steward of the Father the steward of the Son, namely Peter to Moses; and he willed to show the chaste man of old to the chaste man of the new, Elijah to John. Two suns did the disciples behold today on the mountain: one, which was beheld by them all in the firmament, and the other, which, shining more splendidly than it, was seen by the prophets and disciples: the face of Jesus. This Sun which glowed on the mountain illumined by its power that which is in the firmament. For this is the Sun of Justice, burning and shining; by burning he kindles the faithful in himself, by shining he enlightens all. Of this Sun John says: 'He was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world' (John 1:9).

CHAPTER III. — But that his brightness might be made known to us more certainly than certain, after his countenance was transfigured into another appearance, and he was overshadowed with the apostles by a bright cloud, he was truly glorified by the Father: 'This is my dearest Son,' he said, 'listen to him' (Luke 9:35). The disciples, not bearing so great a voice, fell on their faces; and as Moses and Elijah withdrew, the divine offspring alone remained, who, raising them, said, 'Do not be afraid', which is to say: Let those fear who do not believe; let those fear whom phantoms deceive. You who obey the Son of the Father and are present at his hidden secrets, why are you fearful? Yet the holy disciples, looking round, saw no one but Jesus alone; so that it might be clearly shown that the voice which had been sent befitted not Moses, not Elijah, but the only-begotten Son alone. Of this vision a certain most eloquent poet marvels at and praises the merit of these three apostles, saying (Sedulius, book III, line 284 ff.): 'O sublime merit of the three, to whom it befell to see in the world things not entrusted to the world! What of this, that both Elijah and Moses, famed for virtue, unknown to their eyes, they saw by the light of the heart? So that our faith may be greater that he is, throughout the world, the beginning and the end, he, namely, Alpha and Omega, whom in the midst such prophets shone around, the one still living, the other without the light of life; and saying with starry sound, "This is my Son", the Father's voice showed by word that Christ is begotten.'

Hence to Moses, praying and saying, 'Show me your glory,' the Lord says: 'You cannot see my face: for man shall not see me and live. Behold,' he says, 'there is a place by me, and you shall stand upon the rock; and when my glory passes, I will set you in a cleft of the rock, and protect you with my right hand until I pass by, and I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back parts, but my face you cannot see' (Exod. 33:18, 20 ff.). What, dearly beloved, is this? What is this? Has no one ever seen the Lord? Did one of these lie, who said: 'No one has ever seen God, except the Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known' (John 1:18)? Is the almighty Father, incomprehensible and immeasurable and invisible, believed to be corporeal, or are bodily members ascribed to him, so that he is said to have back parts? This is great, this is deep; and for such little ones as we it is not easy to search out something so deep. But it must be opened by him alone who, when he wills, opens the mouth of brute animals to speak. O Holy Spirit, unlock for us this supreme utterance of the Father. Attend more diligently, attend more carefully, dearly beloved, and together with me prepare your minds.

CHAP. IV. 'When I have passed by,' says the Lord, 'you shall see my back parts; my face you cannot see' (Exod. 33:23). For the face of the Lord is the incomprehensible Godhead; but his back parts are to be believed to be the humanity assumed by the Son. Indeed by the face, which is the first part of the body, the Godhead before all ages is signified; but the back parts are the humanity of Christ, which came to us in the last times through the inviolate Mary. On this day, then, what he promised to his servant Moses the Father faithfully fulfilled through the Son. Of this solemnity of this day David says: 'You have put on praise and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment' (Ps. 103:1). Christ put on praise and beauty when he was glorified by the glory of the Father's voice; he was clothed with light as with a garment when he showed his disciples his face flashing with the splendour of the sun. At this solemnity too the prophet Habakkuk marvelled, when he sang: 'Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified' (Hab. 3:1). Was it the fabric of the world that he marvelled at and was terrified? No. But what did he marvel at and was terrified? Hear what follows: 'In the midst,' he says, 'of two living creatures you will be known.' O dearest ones, what is 'to be known in the midst of two living creatures'? What but either in the midst of the two Testaments, or in the midst of Moses and Elijah, conversing with him today on the mountain? For this is the cornerstone, in which each wall was found worthy to be joined, namely the old Testament and the new. The Old is signified by Moses and Elijah, by whom the law and the prophets are designated; the New by Peter and James and John, by whom the holy and venerable Gospel is designated. Or else by Moses and Elijah that former Jewish people, and by Peter, James and John the gentile people is designated. This indeed is the people walking in darkness, which has seen a great light; to the contemplation of which light may the Only-begotten of the Father lead us in that homeland in which the just will shine like the sun, and God himself will be all in all, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, and is glorified, God, through [all ages].
